## 6. A fenced or wiped runtime (finding 3)

**The signal.** `SharedReplicaStore.replaced: StateFlow<Replacement?>`, set once per handle, the
first time any access finds `epoch ≠ base.epoch` (§3.1) or the open finds a newer store (§5.2);
for this process's own wipe it is set by the wiping caller when its flow ends (§5.1).
`Replacement(reason, replacedBy)` reads `meta.replaced_by` and the version tables in the same
transaction: `SKEW` if the store's versions are now above this build's, `UPDATING` if a replacement job
is in progress (`meta.migration`, §5.3, or `meta.wipe`, §5.1; the `Replacement` carries which), otherwise `REPLACED`.
**`CORRUPT`** is set only where the table of §5.2.2 says **CORRUPT**, or on finding the marker (§3.1
step 0). Every other failure is a retry or `COMMIT_FAILED`, a non-persistent signal, per that table. ⚠⚠ Corruption cannot move the epoch (a
corrupt file may not take the write), and a sibling that never touches the damaged pages would
otherwise go on committing unsynced rows. So **the process that detects corruption first writes a
durable marker, `replica/CORRUPT`**, beside the database (a sidecar: it cannot live inside the file
it describes), holding the time, the detecting app and the SQLite error, and **written to survive
power loss** by the sidecar rule below. Only once that sequence has returned is the store reported
durably fenced.

⚠⚠ **The sidecar rule, for every marker or sentinel file this design creates** (*GK*: on iOS
`fsync` does not reach the medium, `fcntl(F_FULLFSYNC)` does; a rename is durable only once its
directory is synced): write a temporary file in the same directory, `F_FULLFSYNC` it, `rename` it
into place, then open the directory and `F_FULLFSYNC` it (`fsync` only where `F_FULLFSYNC` is refused
as **not supported**, never after another failure of it: Appendix B.3 (24); Q0 (q)). Being in `replica/`, it inherits the protection class and backup
exclusion of §2.4. The files it applies to:

| File | Rule |
|---|---|
| `replica/CORRUPT` | the full rule, before the store is reported fenced |
| `replica-damaged/<dir>/COMPLETE` (§6) | the full rule, after every copied file has itself been `F_FULLFSYNC`ed, so an export is offered only if it is all on disk |
| the empty `objects.db` of §5.2 step 0 | `F_FULLFSYNC` the directory after the `O_EXCL` create; a create lost to power loss is simply repeated at the next open, so no temporary file is needed |
| everything else | there is no other: the epoch, sequence, watermark, lease records and version stamps live in the database and take SQLite's durability (`synchronous=FULL`, §2.3) |
 Every process checks it at every outermost access inside the write lock (§3.1 step 0)
and at every open (§5.2 steps 0 and 2), and fences itself `CORRUPT` on finding it. Nothing removes it
automatically: only deleting every Tenshu app (the container goes) or a deliberate repair outside the
app does. A
failed `COMMIT` (§2.5) sets it with `COMMIT_FAILED`, handled as `REPLACED`, except that it rebuilds
**at most once per foreground**: a second failure leaves the runtime fenced on an error state
("storage unavailable"), so a full disk cannot loop rebuilds. **This state is in memory only:** the
next foreground rebuilds again, so a transient I/O error or a full disk that the user clears costs
one foreground, never the store. The only evidence that promotes a commit failure to corruption is the
table's promotion rule (§5.2.2). The `quick_check` runs on a
read-only `CLASSIFY` connection, in the foreground under a token, and only within a bound of 1 s
(although it holds no write lock it holds a **read mark** for its whole run, which is what the
ceiling checkpoint's `B_ckpt` waits for). ⭐ **Q0 (m) has measured it** (results doc §13.2): about
21 µs a page cold and 1.25 µs cached, so 1 s reaches about **47,000 pages, 185 MiB**, cold, and
every page of `MAX_DB_PAGES` cached; the 32 MiB this paragraph used to give was the `VACUUM INTO`
path's placeholder. And it is not one uninterruptible statement on the vendored build, which keeps
the progress callback: slice 3's confirmation stops it at the bound from inside (B.3 (47)). Past
the bound there is no promotion, only "storage unavailable" and a retry, ⚠ **which is a ship
blocker as it stands** (§13, B.2).

**The handle, once fenced** (as in the draft, because it is right): reads return absent; writes and
removals throw `ReplicaReplaced` before touching the database; the transaction is rolled back and
released at once. Reads do not throw because an undeclared Kotlin exception crossing into Swift
aborts the process (lease draft §5.5).

**The owner.** The runtime host that built the graph, which is one class per route: every first-party
app's `*LocalRuntime` assembles through `FirstPartyLocalRuntime.assembleBase`
(`FirstPartyLocalRuntime.kt:81`), and Control through `ControlSurface`. Each subscribes to
`replaced` when it installs a graph. Nobody else acts on it. Both hosts get their handle from the registry (§2.8) and never close one themselves: `ControlSurface`'s live runtime and its store-less wipe (`ControlSurface.kt:1555-1584`) go through the same registry as every `*LocalRuntime`.

**The lifecycle**, on the main thread:

| Step | `REPLACED` | `SKEW` | `CORRUPT` |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Surfaces show **"Refreshing…"** (a state, not the fakes: an empty listing over no store would be an empty success) | Surfaces show the **update surface**, naming **this app** (`core-schema-skew-surface.md`: on iOS route 1 the app to name is the app itself; no update button, no platform route) | Surfaces show **"Storage damaged"**, honestly: Tenshu cannot read its data on this phone; what was already synced is safe on the relay and the user's other devices, but **changes made on this phone that had not synced yet may be lost**; the damaged data has been kept aside and can be exported from Control before anything is reset (below). Read-only, no store access |
| 2 | Stop the old graph: the loops' `stop()`, the wake job cancelled, `SyncManager.lock()` as `deprovision` does (`DriveLocalRuntime.kt:395-407`), **custody kept** | the same | the same |
| 2b | **Release the fenced handle through the registry** (§2.8): roll back if in a transaction, close the connection, remove the handle. A failed rollback, close or release latches the process `UNUSABLE`: "storage unavailable", no step 4 | the same | the same |
| 3 | Only then orphan the old graph until process death (`deprovision`'s precedent); it holds no open handle | the same | the same |
| 4 | ⚠ *Amended by Q48 (decided 2026-10-29), B.17 (254): a `SKEW` or `CORRUPT` met at an **open** gives the graph the stand-in and gives it up; the host does not re-open it in that process (an update relaunches the app; the marker never goes away by itself).* **In the foreground only**, and only once 2b succeeded: first the shipping-gate probe (bridge present? adopted custody left?); bridge gone with custody left → `deprovision()`, not `install()` (§5.1); otherwise `install()` again. The new graph opens a new handle that adopts the current epoch with an empty cache; the surfaces are re-installed and fill from the shared store and the next pull | Nothing is rebuilt. On the next foreground the host re-opens; the open judges the versions (§5.2) and either stays `SKEW` or, after an update, opens | ⭐ *As built (Appendix B.18, 2026-10-30): `ReplicaDamagedSnapshot` and `SharedReplicaDamagedCopies` in `core-common/src/iosSqliteMain`, run by Control's `DamagedSnapshotRunner` at the move into `CORRUPT` and at each foreground; the checkpoint drain is waited before the writer drain (300), `COMPLETE` is written inside the `.partial` and the directory renamed after it (299), a header SQLite cannot read is byte-copied without a hold (301), a copy needs its size plus 256 MiB free (303), and a newer complete copy replaces the older one (305), which this column's "never deleted" now reads as: never deleted by any code but that replacement.* ⭐ *Amended by B.18.8 (2026-10-30, the maintainer's decisions): the paths are tried **backup API, byte copy, then `VACUUM INTO` last** (319: a logical rebuild hides the damage a forensic copy is for); the user may **delete the copy** in Control, after which the same damage is not copied again (320); Control's forget, which then removes it, warns first; and the leftovers are removed at Control's launch and after its forget (316).* **Never rebuilt, never repaired, never deleted or replaced** (S1, D8). **Control preserves the file first, as one consistent snapshot, and the marker makes it final.** Before snapshotting, Control makes sure the marker exists and is durable, then quiets the file in two steps, neither of which is an exclusive lock (**WAL mode has none to offer: `BEGIN EXCLUSIVE` there is `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`**, *GK*, sqlite.org/lang_transaction.html, so nothing Control can hold stops a peer's `PASSIVE` checkpoint from rewriting `objects.db`). **(i) The writer drain:** `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` then `ROLLBACK` on its `SNAPSHOT` connection, which waits for any writer that took the lock before the marker existed to finish; every later writer sees the marker at step 0 and refuses. **(ii) The checkpoint drain:** every checkpoint path checks the marker immediately before it starts and refuses if it is there (§4.2.1, S20), so after the marker is durable no checkpoint can **begin** in any process; one already running is ended by its own deadline, **`CKPT_MAX` = `2 · T(Wmax + δ) + B_ckpt`** (the hold watchdog's, §4.2.1; about 1.7 s at the placeholders), so Control waits until `CKPT_MAX` has passed since the marker's recorded time, once. From then on nothing commits and nothing checkpoints, so a snapshot taken after both drains is the store's final state. (If the writer drain cannot take the lock, path (4) below applies.) The snapshot is taken once per marker; as a cheap belt-and-braces check, `COMPLETE` records the sizes and modification times of `objects.db` **and `-wal`**, and a later foreground that finds them changed takes a new snapshot instead of offering the old one. It runs in the foreground only, into `replica-damaged/<UTC timestamp>/` with the same protection class and backup exclusion (§2.4), never deleted. Control alone does this. **Every snapshot connection is a registered handle (§2.8) of kind `SNAPSHOT`, admitted through the gate, under an explicit protection token for the whole snapshot; quiesce counts, interrupts and closes it like any other.** ⚠⚠ **The one exception to the marker:** a `SNAPSHOT` handle, which only Control's host may create and only after the marker exists, skips §3.1 step 0 and §5.2's classification, for exactly two things: the writer drain (`BEGIN IMMEDIATE`, then `ROLLBACK`, with no statement in between) and the copy (`VACUUM INTO` to the export directory, the backup API, or the byte copy under a writer hold, `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` ended by `ROLLBACK`). Any other statement on it, and every write, throws before reaching SQLite. With close-time checkpointing suppressed (§4.2.1's ship requirement), closing this connection writes nothing to the originals. The export is written to `<dir>.partial/` and renamed to `<dir>/` with a `COMPLETE` marker, written by the sidecar rule above, only when it has finished **and, for a byte copy, been verified** (below); "Export damaged data" offers only complete snapshots, and a `.partial` directory left by an aborted attempt is deleted at the next attempt (it is Control's own temporary copy, never the originals). In order: **(1)** `VACUUM INTO '<dir>.partial/objects.db'` on that connection **in autocommit mode** (SQLite refuses `VACUUM` inside an open transaction, *GK*), which writes from one snapshot by itself whatever peers do (*GK*); it works if the damage leaves the pages it reads readable. ⚠ It is one statement, which no gate check can interrupt (`sqlite3_progress_handler` is absent, §4.2), so it is attempted only when the file is small enough to finish well inside the 2 s expiry drain (a bound Q0 measures; until then, files over 32 MiB skip to (2)). **(2)** If that fails or the file is too large: **the backup API** (`sqlite3_backup_init` from the `SNAPSHOT` connection into `<dir>.partial/objects.db`, then `sqlite3_backup_step` a fixed number of pages at a time, **with a gate check between steps**, then `sqlite3_backup_finish`; *Read*: `nm -gU` shows the bundled library exports all three, and the driver of §2.1.1 reaches them). It copies pages through the pager from one read snapshot, WAL content included, without interpreting any B-tree, so it tolerates damage that stops `VACUUM INTO`, and unlike it, it can be interrupted between steps; it fails when the header or the WAL index cannot be read at all (*GK*). **(3)** If that fails too: **the byte copy, self-verifying.** Control takes a **writer hold** on the `SNAPSHOT` connection, `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`, which blocks writers and a `RESTART` checkpoint and **nothing more** (not a reader, not a `PASSIVE` checkpoint); what keeps checkpoints away is the marker and the checkpoint drain, and what proves it is the check. Inside the hold: record a **fingerprint** of the originals (size and modification time of `objects.db`, `-wal` and `-shm`; a SHA-256 of `objects.db`'s first page, of the `-wal`'s 32-byte header and of the whole `-shm`, which is small and changes whenever a checkpoint or a reader moves); byte-copy `objects.db` and `-wal` **in 1 MiB chunks with a gate check between chunks** (`-shm` is derived and is rebuilt when the copy is opened, *GK*); record the fingerprint again; `ROLLBACK`. **If the two fingerprints differ, the `.partial` is discarded and the copy retried, up to 3 times in one foreground; after that the export is reported as failed** (*"the damaged data could not be copied consistently"*), never as complete. `COMPLETE` is written only for a `VACUUM INTO`, a finished backup, or a byte copy whose fingerprints matched. If protection ends mid-copy, it stops, rolls back and closes the connection through the registry, leaves the `.partial` directory unfinished (never offered), and retries at the next foreground. **(4)** If the writer drain or the writer hold cannot take the lock (a peer holds the file in a transaction) or every path fails: nothing is offered, the files stay in place, untouched and never deleted, the surface says *"the damaged data is still on this phone and has not been copied yet"*, and Control retries at the next foreground. Control's surface offers **"Export damaged data"** (the system share sheet, to Files or AirDrop), which is how the user or the maintainer gets it off the phone to inspect it with `sqlite3`; nothing in the app reads it again. The only destructive step is the user's: deleting every Tenshu app removes the container, preserved copy included, so the surface says to export first if anything was unsynced. On each foreground the host re-opens once; the read-only classification (§5.2 step 2) either finds it still unreadable (the surface stays) while the marker exists the store stays fenced, even if something outside the app repaired the file, until the marker is removed with it. A wake ends `finished = false` |
| In the background | steps 1–3 (2b included); step 4 waits for the foreground, or the next wake's `ensureRuntime` builds a new graph (lease draft §7.5 step 4) | steps 1–3 (2b included) | steps 1–3 (2b included) |

**`UPDATING`** (a migration or a wipe in progress, §5.3, §5.1; every wipe passes through it, D13) runs `REPLACED`'s steps 1–3,
with the surface **"Updating storage…"** for a migration and **"Refreshing…"** for a wipe. Step 4
differs: a host whose build can resume the job (§5.2 step 2: a migration, at or above the marker's
`to` and in the foreground; a wipe, any build that does not judge the store newer, in the foreground
or in a wake under its token) runs it on a `REPLACEMENT` handle under a token on a background
thread, then installs (after a wipe, through `REPLACED`'s step 4 probe); any other host in the
foreground waits, re-opening at each foreground and at each epoch change (a migration chain's Finish and a
wipe's last chunk both move the epoch), and installs once the marker is gone; a build that cannot
read the result shows the update surface, as for `SKEW`, **and so does a host whose running job
finds at a chunk that it no longer qualifies** (§5.3's marker rule: its `REPLACEMENT` handle is
fenced `SKEW`, having written nothing). In the background, a migration waits
(`StoreNeedsForeground`); a wipe may be resumed by a wake under its token.

The wake that was running when its handle was fenced ends `finished = false`, as the draft's exit
table already says (its §7.5). What the user sees: after Control's device-forget, the sibling apps
show "Refreshing…" and then the state of the realm they are in (their own deprovision follows from
the Keychain, which is outside this design); after a newer sibling migrated, an older app shows
"Update <app>" at its next store access, mid-session if it is open.

## 7. Schema skew across apps (M12)

**The situation.** One store, ten apps, and the App Store updates them one at a time. *Read:* today
an older build that finds a newer store **deletes every row**, unlocked
(`FileObjectStore.kt` open, lease draft §5.7), and the JVM store does the same on
`recorded > current` (`SqliteObjectStore.kt:1266-1296`). On iOS route 1 every app opens the store
itself and nothing enforces lockstep (`core-schema-evolution.md` §2, the lockstep fact is Android's).

SQLite changes the costs: a wipe and a migration each run behind a fence that
every process honours (§5.1, §5.3); the versions are rows read
in the same transaction as the decision; and a replacement already moves `epoch`, which every live
process checks at its next access.

| Option | With SQLite | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| (a) Refuse a newer store, show the update surface | the open reads the versions through a read-only connection and re-reads them under its write transaction (§5.2 steps 2 and 2a); costs the split of "newer than me" from "below my floor", which share a wipe today | right, but alone it misses a sibling **already running** when the store is migrated |
| (b) Migrate only when every installed app can read the result | needs a table of installed apps and their versions; an uninstalled app's row blocks the newest app for ever, and one app cannot enumerate another's installation (*GK*); the newer app still cannot read old rows while it waits | rejected |
| (c) A minimum-version marker every app honours at open and at catch-up | with SQLite the marker **is** the version stamps already in the file (`user_version`, `schema_service_versions`, `meta.layout`), and "at catch-up" is the epoch change every migration makes. Under House Rule 9 every reshape is breaking, so a separate "minimum reader" value would always equal the stamps | folds into (a) |
| (d) Keep today's wipes, made safe | a wipe is now seconds of bounded chunks and crash-safe (§5.1); still ping-pongs between skewed apps, and each wipe deletes the unsynced outbound queue | rejected beyond test data |

**Recommendation (D5, accepted 2026-10-03): (a) with (c)'s trigger.**

1. A build never writes to, migrates or wipes a store with any recorded version above its own:
   `user_version`, any service in `schema_service_versions` (a service this build does not know
   counts as above), or `meta.layout`. It opens fenced `SKEW` (§6).
2. The check runs at open and **whenever the epoch changes** (§3.1 step 2), which every migration
   and wipe does. So a running older sibling is fenced at its very next access, not at its next
   launch.
3. A newer build migrates an older store in resumable chunks behind the "updating" fence (§5.3,
   D11), or wipes it below its floor in budgeted chunks behind the same fence (§5.1, D13),
   started in the foreground, and moves the epoch.
4. Nothing is lost: an older app's unsynced outbound rows are in the shared store, migrated with
   everything else, and pushed by the newer app (the relay accepts old-format writes, the asymmetric
   contract of `core-schema-evolution.md` §7.3).
5. The newest app always proceeds, so there is no deadlock; the cost is that an out-of-date app is
   unusable until updated, which is the posture of the cross-device fence (§7.3 there).

⚠ It protects only builds that contain the check, so it must be in the first build that opens
`replica/objects.db`. That is free: no build without the check can reach this database. The
pre-App-Group builds use app-local file stores, and the App Group builds on the maintainer's phone
today (§8) use the shared `FileObjectStore` under `objects/`, not `replica/`; neither opens SQLite. ⭐ Accepted by the maintainer, 2026-10-03 (D5).

## 8. Moving to it

**The baseline this cutover was designed against** (*Read*, `ios-background-scheduling.md` §4.1.1,
as of 2026-10-02): S0 merged, no App Group build installed on a device; each app keeps an app-local
`FileObjectStore` that `reclaimLegacyAppLocalReplica()` removes only when empty and otherwise keeps
and reports; on the test phone Control, Drive, Fit and Photos held about 2,500, 31,000, 1,100 and
2,900 rows. For a device in that state **there is no file-store-to-SQLite migration**: the first
SQLite build writes `replica/objects.db` only, and no `FileObjectStore` exists in its group
container. The steps and the paragraphs below are written for that baseline.

⚠⚠ **The observed state of the maintainer's phone is not that baseline** (2026-10-06, from its
crash logs, §4.1): App Group builds of the real apps are installed and **already share one
`FileObjectStore` replica in the group container**, under the hand-built lock. How the phone got
there is not recorded, and whether the drain, the stranded app-local stores and the watermark went
as the steps below describe is **not known**. So "a `FileObjectStore` has never existed in a
device's group container" is false for this phone, and the row counts above describe stores that
may no longer be the live ones.

⭐ **Decided by the maintainer 2026-11-01: route (b), wipe and re-sync; built in S0b-4 slice 1
(Appendix B.20).** Control drains the old store on the file store, proves from the shared queues on
disk that nothing in it is this device's alone, then retires `objects/` and `sync-hlc/` together
under the file store's `flock` and rebuilds over the SQLite store from cursor 0; the apps wait on
the file store until Control declares `sqlite`. The paragraph below is the item as it was opened.

⚠⚠ **Open item for the phase that builds the cutover (S0b-4), not designed here: a device already
on the shared file store.** (Until 2026-10-11 Drive on that phone was installed as
`app.tenshu.drive.ios2`, a local stopgap while the original id was held by the personal team; it
is `app.tenshu.drive.ios` again and the `.ios2` app is gone, so the cutover has one Drive and one
id to consider — [`ios-background-scheduling.md`](ios-background-scheduling.md) §4.1.1.) The
cutover must handle it, by one of two routes, and the choice is
left to that phase: **(a) migrate** the shared `FileObjectStore` replica into the SQLite store
(a file-store-to-SQLite importer, which this design otherwise does not have, with its own answer
for the watermark's identity binding, §5.4); or **(b) wipe and re-sync**: drain as in step 1,
create the empty SQLite store, pull from cursor 0, and remove the old `objects/` and its watermark
(the reclaimer's group-container case below, which so far was written for the simulator only).
Either way the old shared file store must not be left beside the new one with a watermark older
than its store. The lock that file store runs under today is what is being killed with
`0xdead10cc` (§4.1).

| Step | Who | What |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Drain | the person with the phone, on the **current** builds | Open each app online until sync is idle and uploads have finished. ⚠ Control's realm must be registered with a relay first: a realm with no relay copy strands everything (S0 inventory). Pending moves and queued one-shot schedule items are stranded too; the S0 inventory lists every plane |
| 2. Install | | All App Group builds **from one commit**, so the first state has no skew |
| 3. Launch Control first | | It owns provisioning; it creates the empty store and pulls from cursor 0 |
| 4. Launch the others | | They open the same store; legacy app-local stores report `KEPT` |
| 5. Discard | after checking step 1 | Launch each app once with `TENSHU_DISCARD_LEGACY_REPLICA=1`, or delete and reinstall |

**Re-synced or re-derived:** realm rows, device settings and the three cursors (they are rows); the
HLC watermark (`meta.hlc_watermark`, §5.4) starts **empty, never seeded from an app-local
`sync-hlc` file**. That file records no identity, and continuity cannot be proven: a phone that
forgot and re-provisioned before the upgrade kept the file, and the new identity's runtime then
raised the same file, so even a file written after the current custody was created can hold the old
identity's high value. Carrying it could publish that value into the new slot, which §5.4 refuses.
The cost, accepted: the first tip from the shared store may be below what the device's slot already
holds, so peers show `DIVERGENCE` for this device **until its tip passes the old value**, which
happens at its first local write (its physical time is the current wall clock) or when the cutover's
re-pull has ingested the blocks that tip came from; the tracker clears itself then
(`HlcDivergenceTracker.kt:36-40`). Once per device, at a cutover the maintainer times. This keeps the
S0 inventory's "not carried over on purpose"; thumbnails, cached bytes and
offline pins re-fetch; map region bytes must be removed and downloaded again (their index is in the
Keychain); Calendar re-arms reminders at its next reconcile. **Stranded if not drained:** everything
the S0 inventory marks so.

**On the simulator** (and, as observed, on the maintainer's phone: the open item above) the group
container may hold an old `objects/` file store and `sync-hlc/` from earlier runs. The reclaimer gains a group-container case (file operations on the old file-store paths only;
it never opens or touches `replica/`, so it needs no connection) that removes the old `objects/` and the
watermark beside it when the SQLite store is created, because a watermark older than its store
forges the tombstone-GC acknowledgement (S0 inventory). Simulator data is test data; whether this
removal is the right treatment of a real device's shared file store is route (b) of the open item.
⭐ *It is (decided 2026-11-01), once the drain is proven: `LegacyFileStoreCutover`, B.20.*

`FileObjectStore`, `wipeFileObjectStore`, `readObjectStoreEntries`, `SharedReplicaDatabaseLock`,
`HlcWatermarkFile`, `FileAdvisoryLock` (§5.4) and the two downcasts are deleted ~~in S0b-4~~ ⚠ **in a
hotfix after Control-iOS 1.0's App Store approval** (decided by the maintainer 2026-11-01; B.20.6,
`tech-debt.md`), once nothing binds them.

## 9. What it removes from the draft, and what the lease and scheduler change

### 9.1 Draft §5, mechanism by mechanism

| Draft §5 mechanism | Fate | Now |
|---|---|---|
| `replica.writer.lock` + `flock`, blocking | **removed** | WAL write lock via `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` (engine) |
| The tried store lock (1 ms → 20 ms) | **changed** | the same loop around `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` with a 50 ms busy slice (§4.2) |
| Rule D (never unlink, `fstat` link count) | **removed** | S1: no file replacement exists; SQLite owns its files |
| `replica.generation` (`instance`, `generation`), `pread`/`pwrite`, short-write rule | **removed** | `meta.epoch` and `meta.seq`, written in the writer's own transaction (engine atomicity) |
| Advance-before-change | **removed** | one transaction: no order |
| Rule C (intent, distrust, change, clear) and its crash table | **removed** | WAL rollback; one transaction per change |
| `replica.wiping`, the staged migration's commit marker, staging directory | **replaced** | no marker files and no staging directory. For every wipe and every migration, a marker **row** (`meta.wipe`, `meta.migration`) fences the store as "updating" while budgeted chunks run on a `REPLACEMENT` handle (D11, D13, §5.1, §5.3) |
| Recovery completes a dead process's intent | **changed** | nothing to complete for an ordinary transaction (WAL rollback). A chunked migration or wipe left by a dead process is resumed from its marker by the next qualifying open (§5.2 step 2); the epoch does not move on a resume |
| The fence | **kept**, with its semantics | §6, plus the owner and lifecycle it lacked |
| Full rehydrate as catch-up | **changed** | cache drop + listened-row re-read (§3.3) |
| `SharedContainerLockGate`, tokens, quiesce, rule P | **kept** | §4; quiesce also closes the runtime's connection and releases every job handle (§2.8's table), with close-time checkpointing suppressed on every connection (mandatory, Q0 (j)); rule P as a predicate (§4.4) |
| 1 s hold ceiling and long-hold log | **kept** | a wipe is chunks, each under 1 s and interruptible (D13), so finding 2 is gone; the exceptions are the ceiling checkpoint (on its own connection, outside any transaction) and an open's index rebuild, bounded by `Wmax` (S8) |
| Chunked wipe (S0b-2 row) | **kept, in SQLite's terms** | **every wipe is a resumable chunked wipe** (D13, 2026-10-06): `meta.wipe` and a new epoch in the first chunk, budgeted single-row delete chunks on a `REPLACEMENT` handle, the last chunk clearing the marker and moving the epoch (§5.1, R3). An interim revision ran a small store's wipe as one truncate-optimised `DELETE`; Q0 showed that statement uninterruptible and seconds long when uncached, and it was removed |
| `open` under the lock | **changed** | a read-only classification, then one write transaction (§5.2) |
| `HlcWatermarkFile` through the gate | **changed** | `meta.hlc_watermark`, raised in a transaction, bound to the identity and kept across same-identity wipes, plus one identity-bound Keychain item per app, read before and raised after that transaction, never inside it (§5.4, D9 and its amendment) |
| `IosFileDatabase` outside the layers | **kept** | unchanged; its ranged-write hazard stays in lease draft §14 |

### 9.2 The lease moves into the database (D6, accepted)

The draft's lease is a file per key written inside the store lock (its §4.2). With the store a
SQLite database, the record becomes a row of `schedule_lease`, and **rule A becomes one SQLite
transaction**: read the `PENDING` registry row from `objects`, read and write the lease row, commit.

| Draft §4 item | With the lease in the database |
|---|---|
| Separate locks between the registry and the lease (the class v0.7 removed by hand) | gone by construction: one transaction, one lock |
| `sched-lease/` directory, SHA-256 file names, 255-byte limit, W23 | gone: `key` is the primary key, capped at 512 bytes by the store (`LeaseKeyTooLong`, §4.2.1) |
| Whole-file temp-and-rename writes | an `UPDATE` in the transaction |
| Wipe removing records after the new instance (draft W18) | deleted by chunks of the same wipe as the rows, behind `meta.wipe`: no access reads a lease row between the wipe's first chunk and its last (§5.1) |
| T16 causes | the store is unavailable or fenced, or `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` was not obtained within one `HEARTBEAT`; outcomes unchanged (fail closed) |
| M4 (lease directory unusable) | the same as the store being unusable: nothing runs |
| `peek` lock-free | a read in its own short transaction |
| State machine, R1–R5, T1–T16, `waitMs`, clock rules, I1, I5, I6, I8 | **unchanged** |

The interface stays `ScheduleRunLease` in `:sync-service-proxy` commonMain. The iOS binding
(`FileRunLease` in the draft's §7.1) becomes a `ReplicaRunLease` over a `LeaseTable` the store
exposes, which asserts it is called inside a transaction and **never caches a lease row** (every
call reads the table, so `seq` need not cover it). A heartbeat commits every 10 s and moves
siblings' `data_version`, but not `seq` (S4), so they read `meta` and keep their caches.

### 9.3 Scheduler (draft §7) and sub-phases

- §7.5 step 9 and `expire()`: quiesce now closes the connection; `expire()` follows §4.4 (cancel the
  wake, end its token, shut down only if `protected` became false).
- §7.5 exit table: "the handle is fenced mid-wake" stands.
- §11.4 step 1 now tests SQLite's locks, not `flock` (§13 Q0).
- §12: S0b-1 to S0b-3 of the draft are replaced by §13 here; S1a-2's `LeaseRecordFile` becomes the
  `LeaseTable`. S1a–S1c are otherwise unchanged.

## 10. Invariants

| # | Invariant | Rests on |
|---|---|---|
| **S1** | **SQLite owns its files.** Nothing but a SQLite connection opens, renames, truncates, replaces or unlinks `objects.db`, `-wal` or `-shm`. Two exceptions: the `O_CREAT | O_EXCL` creation of an empty `objects.db` when none exists (§5.2 step 0), which can never truncate or replace a file; and Control's snapshot of a `CORRUPT` store into `replica-damaged/` (§6), taken through SQLite or as a byte copy verified by fingerprint, which reads the originals and writes nothing to them. | §2.7; engine |
| **S2** | **One access, one transaction.** Every outermost store access, from `DatabaseImpl` or not, is one `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` … `COMMIT`; no statement or transaction survives the outermost exit. | §2.5; autocommit assertion |
| **S3** | **No stale base.** No access reads or writes from a resident base older than the store's last foreign commit. | §3.2: write lock held from the check to commit; S4 |
| **S4** | **Changes announce themselves atomically.** Every transaction that writes `objects` moves `meta.seq` in that transaction; every replacement writes a new random `meta.epoch` in its start and in its finish (§5.3's epoch rule; a wipe's first and last chunks, a migration chain's Start and Finish), never in a resume or a chunk between them. A version stamp changes only between a migration chain's Start and its Finish, so those two epochs announce it; an intermediate step's stamp moves none, the store being fenced "updating" throughout. | §3.1, §5 |
| **S5** | **No lock without protection, and no connection outside the registry.** No close ever checkpoints (§4.2.1's ship requirement), and no checkpoint runs without a token or beyond the time it has left. Every connection to the shared database, of every handle kind §2.8 lists (the runtime's, `CLASSIFY`, store-less wipe, `CHECKPOINT`, `REPLACEMENT`, `SNAPSHOT`), is opened and closed through the registry and admitted through the gate (§2.8). A thread is in a transaction, or holds an open statement, on the shared database only while admitted by the gate; no connection is open once the gate has closed and drained, and what quiesce does to each handle kind is §2.8's table, stated there only. Every checkpoint and other uninterruptible call under a token has §4.2.1's hard stop, or the cap that needs sign-off. | §4.2, §4.3, §4.2.1 |
| **S6** | **Protection is a predicate.** The gate is open exactly while `isForeground || liveTokens ≠ ∅`; an expiry ends tokens, never the foreground's protection. | §4.4 |
| **S7** | **Waiting holds nothing.** A thread waiting on a sibling waits at most 50 ms inside SQLite per slice and re-meets the gate between slices; nothing blocks in the kernel for a container lock. | §4.2; *GK* (non-blocking `fcntl`) |
| **S8** | **Bounded holds in the background, and cancellable replacements.** A migration runs as chunks, each one transaction under 1 s and `TX_BUDGET`, with a gate check between chunks; **every wipe runs the same way** (D13, §5.1): budgeted chunks of single-row deletes with the same gate check between them (resumable in a wake, S13), and no unconditional `DELETE` of a table, which an interrupt cannot reach. **No transaction holds the write lock past `HOLD_MAX` = 1 s up to its commit: the hold watchdog (§4.2.1) interrupts a running statement at the deadline and refuses the next one, and rule (a) follows. The commit's sync is not interruptible and is residual R2; a single-row statement is not interruptible part-way, so its time is bounded by `ROW_MAX` (Q0 (ac)).** The one statement that touches many pages under the lock, an `incremental_vacuum` run, has a size bound derived from a measured time (its `n`), and every chunk loop also stops at 500 ms (§4.2.1). **Two exceptions:** the ceiling checkpoint, which runs **outside any transaction on its own `CHECKPOINT` connection** (the writer that triggered it has rolled its `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` back first, rule 1) and, being `RESTART`, takes SQLite's writer lock itself for at most `T(Wmax + δ) + B_ckpt` (a `PASSIVE` checkpoint takes no writer lock at all); and a connection open's possible index rebuild, `R(Wmax + δ)`. Both are constants with §4.2.1's hard stop; holds over 500 ms are logged with their label. | §4.2, §4.2.1; S13 |
| **S9** | **Crash atomicity.** Whatever instant a process dies, the store is as of its last commit, and no peer ever observed part of a transaction. | engine (WAL) |
| **S10** | **`transaction { }` keeps its meaning.** An exception thrown by the caller commits what was written, as on every platform; a failed `COMMIT` or any failed statement rolls back, and then the handle is fenced `COMMIT_FAILED` (in memory, never the durable marker) and its runtime rebuilt, at most once per foreground and again at the next, because notifications for the rolled-back writes have already been delivered. | §2.5, §6 |
| **S11** | **Nothing is written past a replacement.** A handle whose `base.epoch` differs from the store's writes nothing, and its runtime host replaces or parks its graph. | §6 |
| **S12** | **No build touches a newer store.** A build writes to `objects.db` or `-wal`, migrates or wipes only a store whose every recorded version is at or below its own (it may rebuild a newer store's `-shm`, S19); checked at open and at every epoch change. **A marker never widens this:** a store that is "updating" is judged by the same full check (every recorded stamp, listed in the marker or not) before the marker is read, so no older build resumes a migration or a wipe on a newer store (§5.2 step 2's resumer rule), **and the same check is re-applied at the start of every chunk, to the marker as read under that chunk's write lock** (§5.3's marker rule), so a resumer admitted earlier cannot outlive a change to the chain. | §5.2, §5.3, §7 |
| **S13** | **Replacements need the foreground to start.** A migration (started or resumed) and a below-floor wipe at open run only in the foreground; a background open of a store that needs one fails with `StoreNeedsForeground` without touching it. **The one exception: resuming a wipe** (`meta.wipe`, §5.1; every wipe is resumable, D13), which a wake may run under its token, because the decision to wipe was committed with its first chunk and each further chunk only finishes it. A wipe's **first** chunk is never a wake's: a below-floor wipe starts at a foreground open, and every other wipe is started by the user. | §5.2, §5.1 |
| **S14** | **Elsewhere, nothing changes in behaviour.** The JVM, Android and JS stores and locks are untouched; the lease defaults of the draft's I4 stand. The common-code changes this design makes (`setArrayListener`'s `onReset` and the dangling-member skip, §3.3; the migrator's `pagesOfTypes` and `StepSink`, §5.3; `forgetThisDevice(storeWiped)`, §5.1; `mergedHlc` letting `TipNotPersisted` through, §5.4) are inert or identical off iOS, and their existing tests must pass unchanged. | §2.1, §3.3, §5.1, §5.3 |
| **S15** | **One transaction for row and lease.** A lease decision and the registry row it depends on are read and written in one SQLite transaction. | §9.2 |
| **S16** | **At rest as declared.** `replica/` carries `CompleteUntilFirstUserAuthentication` and the backup exclusion, asserted at every open. | §2.4 |
| **S17** | **Own commits update own state; a self-initiated replacement fences its own handle before its commit returns.** Every commit on a handle's own connection (which its `data_version` never reports) updates or drops that handle's resident state in the same critical section, before `base` moves; a live wipe clears the whole LRU and listener snapshots in its first chunk's critical section. | §2.6 |
| **S18** | **No unreachable connection.** Every logical `SharedReplicaStore` handle is registered in the process-wide registry for as long as its graph is live, and every connection is opened only through the registry on an admitted access. Quiesce treats each handle kind as §2.8's table says (the runtime handle closed and kept, every job handle released); a fence, a failed open, a teardown and the store-less wipe release the handle (rollback if in a transaction, close, remove) before its graph is orphaned or the call returns. No graph is orphaned holding a registered handle, and no live handle is created while another is registered on the same path, except the short-lived job handles §2.8 lists, each released when its operation ends or at quiesce, whichever comes first (§2.8's table). The registry is per process, so a crashed process leaves no handle behind. A failed rollback, close or release latches the process unusable until it succeeds or the process restarts. | §2.8, §4.3, §6 |
| **S19** | **Compatibility before any persistent write.** An open classifies the store (fresh, unreadable, compatible, updating or newer) from the frozen bootstrap marker alone, through a genuinely read-only connection (`SQLITE_OPEN_READONLY`), and opens a read/write connection only once the store is judged fresh, compatible, or updating with a job this build may resume, which requires the full compatibility check first (§5.2 step 2's resumer rule). On a store it has not so judged, a build never changes `objects.db` or `-wal`, never runs a checkpoint and never issues a persistent pragma, `CREATE`, `ALTER` or migration; it **may create or rebuild `-shm`**, which holds no data and which every later opener revalidates against the WAL. The judgement is re-read under the write transaction. | §5.2 |
| **S20** | **Corruption fences every process durably, and only corruption does.** The marker is written by the sidecar rule (temporary file, `F_FULLFSYNC`, rename, directory sync) and the store is reported fenced only after it. The only handle that passes the marker is Control's `SNAPSHOT` handle, for the writer drain and the copy, never for a write. The marker is written only where the table of §5.2.2 says CORRUPT, never on any of its retry or `COMMIT_FAILED` rows. The first process to detect it writes `replica/CORRUPT` before anything else; every outermost access checks it inside the write lock and every open checks it, so no commit begins after it exists; **every checkpoint path (the ceiling `RESTART`, the opportunistic `PASSIVE`, the rewind write) checks it immediately before starting and refuses**, so no checkpoint begins after it exists either. Control's snapshot follows a writer drain and a wait of `CKPT_MAX` for a checkpoint already running, and a byte copy is offered only if the originals' fingerprints were identical before and after it. No exclusive lock is involved: WAL mode has none. | §3.1 step 0, §6 |
| **S21** | **The WAL ceiling (D11).** No WAL file any process can meet exceeds `Wmax + δ`. Every row operation `ROW_MAX` allows fits in one transaction (a transaction begins only at or below `Wmax − δ`, and `δ = C + H` covers the largest single statement). Every writer checkpoints (`RESTART`) and rewinds before a transaction once the WAL has passed `Wmax − δ`, and **no transaction begins until the reset is verified** (the `-wal` back at or below `Wmax − δ`, which only a restart can do); otherwise the write is refused with the retryable `WalResetPending`. **A transaction's growth is measured, not summed:** every connection caps its page cache at `C` pages so that dirty pages spill into the `-wal` as the transaction runs, and before every single-row statement the store admits it only if `wal + C + h ≤ Wmax`, `h` being one statement's loose headroom (`G` plus twice its overflow pages, the depths behind `G` bounded by an enforced `MAX_DB_PAGES`, a write past which is refused with `StoreFull`); otherwise `TransactionBudgetExceeded`, and a row over `ROW_MAX` on any table is `RowTooLarge`, a lease key over 512 bytes `LeaseKeyTooLong`. `Wmax ≥ 2δ`; a migration and every wipe are chunked to the measured budget (D13: no wipe runs as one statement, so nothing is admitted on an estimate); a `stat` after each commit checks the bound. So every open's index rebuild and every checkpoint is bounded by a constant, with no size check before it. ⚠ Relation arrays must be re-stored first (an S0b blocker, §4.2.1); ⭐ *stored in segments by B.19 (2026-10-30), so a list write is admitted as a whole before its first statement and every single-member change fits from the ceiling (B.19.4).* | §4.2.1, §5.1, §5.3 |

## 11. Failure and crash cases

"Peer" is any other process with the store open.

| # | Case | What happens | What a peer observes |
|---|---|---|---|
| F1 | Process dies mid-transaction | uncommitted frames discarded at the next connection's recovery (*GK*) | `seq` unchanged: keeps its cache. Consistent |
| F2 | Process dies after `COMMIT`, before returning | committed | `seq` moved: catches up |
| F3 | Process dies mid-wipe | **in the first chunk** (before its `COMMIT`): rolled back, no marker, the caller saw no success. **After it** (every wipe is chunked, §5.1, D13): **the caller still saw no success**, because the wipe call returns only after the last chunk (`WipeableObjectStore.kt:33-35`), so no discard was reported and no custody purged; the chunk in flight rolls back; the committed chunks, `meta.wipe` and its epoch stay | first chunk: nothing changed. After it: **updating (wipe)**: no app can read the store until the next open of any build that does not judge the store newer resumes it on a `REPLACEMENT` handle, in the foreground or in a wake, and its last chunk clears `meta.wipe` and moves the epoch (§5.1, §5.2; residual R3) |
| F3b | Process dies mid-migration | the chunk in flight is rolled back; the committed chunks, the marker (its targets, current step, phase and cursor), its epoch and the bookkeeping rows stay (§5.3) | every open classifies **updating (migration)**, **between two steps of a chain and during a cleanup phase too**: a build at or above the marker's targets resumes from the current step's phase and cursor in the foreground; an older build shows the update surface; until then the store is unusable to all (accepted, D11) |
| F3c | An older app opens while a newer build's migration is in progress | classified **updating (migration)**, its version below one of the marker's targets, **or below any recorded stamp the marker does not list** (§5.2 step 2's resumer rule): fenced `SKEW`, no write | the migrating app is unaffected |
| F4 | Process killed holding the write lock (`0xdead10cc`, jetsam) | the OS releases its locks; the next connection recovers the WAL | its `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` succeeds after the kill; sees the last commit |
| F5 | Process suspended holding the lock despite the gate (`TimedOut`) and **not** killed | (should not happen: Apple's rule kills it) | waits in slices, logs after 10 s, does not time out into an empty success. The draft's M10 reasoning stands |
| F6 | `COMMIT` fails (disk full, I/O) | rolled back; the access throws; the handle is fenced `COMMIT_FAILED`, **no marker**; the runtime rebuilds once per foreground, and again at the next foreground (§6) | nothing changed; siblings unaffected |
| F6b | A live wipe in this process, with rows in its LRU and a task of its graph waiting for the lock | the LRU and listener snapshots cleared and the handle fenced inside the wipe's first chunk's critical section (S17); the waiting task finds it fenced: no old row rewritten, no watermark raised | fenced at its next access |
| F6c | A fenced handle's block calls `addToArray` | `DatabaseImpl` pre-moves `arraySnapshots` and the write then throws (`ReplicaReplaced`); the graph is discarded by the rebuild | nothing written |
| F6d | A fence (any reason) while the handle's connection is open, or mid-transaction after a failed `COMMIT` | step 2b: rollback, close, release, before the graph is orphaned; `install()` follows | the write lock is free once the rollback runs; no lock survives a later suspension |
| F6e | That rollback, close or release itself fails | the registry latches `UNUSABLE`: no store access, no rebuild, "storage unavailable"; retried on the next foreground or protection grant | a held lock is freed by the retry or by the process's death (§4.1 `TimedOut`) |
| F6f | A same-identity wipe (below-floor, or a reset corrupt store) | `meta.hlc_watermark` is kept; every process rebuilds; the next tip each publish computes is never below the relay's slot | no `DIVERGENCE` from the wipe (send order across apps: §15.1 R4); the slot may over-acknowledge until the re-pull passes it (§5.4 option (i), bounded) |
| F6g | `meta.hlc_watermark` holds a malformed frame (§5.4's definition: wrong format byte, any truncated field, a length out of range, invalid UTF-8, trailing bytes) | decoded as `Stamp.NONE`, logged, overwritten by the next raise (§5.4) | the device publishes no higher acknowledgement until a valid raise; never a forged one |
| F6t | Every Tenshu app is deleted and reinstalled (or a crash follows a publish); the reinstall gate continues as the same device | the new store's watermark is empty; the first publish floors from the maximum of `meta` and every bound per-app item, and that maximum is at least every tip ever published, because each app raised its own item to its tip before the request left (§5.4, D9 amendment); deleting every app removed no item. **First write:** on a fresh install with no item for this app, step 1 reads `Stamp.NONE` for it, `SecItemUpdate` returns `errSecItemNotFound` and `SecItemAdd` creates it; an item bound to another identity reads `Stamp.NONE` and is overwritten; neither blocks the first pull | no computed tip below one already published (arrival order across apps: §15.1 R4), and the first publish is never refused for want of an item; today's code restarts the tip here |
| F6h | Forget this device, then a new setup on the same phone | the wipe keeps the watermark; the new identity's first raise finds the old binding and starts from `NONE` | the new slot starts honest; the old slot is the retired device's |
| F6i | Forget this device | the bridge is cleared before the wipe; the wipe's first chunk fences the handle, and the same call then deletes the rows, the cursors among them (they are rows), in chunks on a `REPLACEMENT` handle, **returning only after the last chunk**; siblings meeting the epoch probe, find no bridge and deprovision; only after the wipe returned does `forgetThisDevice(storeWiped = true)` skip its cursor write and purge custody store-less; only then is `replaced` published and the graph rebuilt over the empty store | nothing touches the fenced handle. **Interrupted mid-wipe** (a kill, or `WipeNotFinished`): custody is not purged, the result is "not finished", a later open finishes the wipe but not the forget; the device holds its identity over an empty store (D3's recoverable half) with its row already retired at the relay, and the user repeats the forget, which is idempotent and completes in every case; if they only reopen the app, an A1 holder re-admits itself and a joiner stays fenced at the relay (§5.1, accepted 2026-10-06) |
| F6j | A reader pins the WAL while writers commit | the opportunistic `PASSIVE` checkpoints copy what they can and leave the rest; at `Wmax − δ` the ceiling `RESTART` waits for the reader in 50 ms slices for at most `B_ckpt`, and the write waiting on it is deferred until the `-wal` is verified reset, refused with `WalResetPending` if it is not; no commit and no quiesce ever runs a checkpoint | the WAL never passes `Wmax`: a pinned reader delays writes (under 1 s for any ordinary access) instead of letting them append past the ceiling |
| F6k | The app is backgrounded during a corrupt-store snapshot | the chunked copy stops at the next gate check, releases its lock and closes through the registry; `VACUUM INTO` was only attempted for files small enough to finish inside the drain (⭐ *as built, B.18 (304): the check is the gate, the foreground and the token's expiry, between every chunk and backup step and inside `VACUUM INTO` by the progress handler*) | the `.partial` export is never offered; retried at the next foreground (⭐ *restarted, not resumed: the `.partial` is deleted first*) |
| F6l | The app is backgrounded in the middle of a migration or a wipe | the run stops between chunks, its marker and committed chunks kept (F9e); its WAL is under `Wmax` by S21, whatever chunk it stopped at. Quiesce never checkpoints and no close checkpoints (§4.2.1) | any later open's rebuild is bounded by the constant `R(Wmax + δ)` |
| F6m | `COMMIT` fails twice in one foreground | `quick_check` on a read-only connection, below the size bound: `ok` keeps the non-persistent "storage unavailable" and retries next foreground; not `ok` writes the marker (F12). Above the bound: no promotion | only a validated corruption fences them (S20) |
| F6n | A statement fails inside an access (any code), whether or not SQLite kept the transaction open | rolled back; handled as `COMMIT_FAILED` (fence, rebuild), because `arraySnapshots`, the cache and the listeners may already hold the change; not a marker | nothing changed |
| F6o | A transient `SQLITE_IOERR` during the open's read-only classification | `StoreUnavailable`, retried next foreground (§5.2.2); no marker | nothing |
| F6p | Apps are never foregrounded; wakes keep writing | each writer checkpoints and rewinds before a transaction once the WAL has passed `Wmax − δ`, and each wake checkpoints at its end past `Wmax/4`; a checkpoint that backfilled every frame rewinds the file with one trivial write, and at the ceiling no write begins until the reset is verified | the WAL never exceeds `Wmax + δ` (S21) |
| F6q | A background wake opens the store after every connection had closed, near token expiry, while a sibling has just committed | the WAL is under `Wmax + δ` whatever the sibling did (S21), so the open's rebuild costs at most the constant `R(Wmax + δ)`; with less protected time than that left, the open is deferred | no rebuild ever starts that could outlive the token, and no size check can go stale |
| F6r | A transaction tries to write more than `TX_BUDGET` (a caller that did not chunk) | the statement that would pass the budget is refused before SQLite with `TransactionBudgetExceeded`, rolled back and fenced `COMMIT_FAILED` (rule (a)) | the WAL never passed `Wmax + δ`; the post-commit `stat` stays quiet |
| F6u | One statement runs past `HOLD_MAX` with protection to spare (a cold cache, a pathological plan), or a caller's block idles past it | the hold watchdog interrupts the running statement (`SQLITE_INTERRUPT`), or refuses the next one and the `COMMIT` (`HoldCeilingExceeded`); rolled back, rule (a): fenced `COMMIT_FAILED`, rebuilt once per foreground. A commit sync already started is not stopped (R2) | siblings waiting on the lock get it after at most `HOLD_MAX` plus the interrupt latency (Q0 (ac)) |
| F6s | A peer syncs a contact whose `rawVcard` exceeds `ROW_MAX` | refused with `RowTooLarge` before SQLite, rule (a); deterministic, so it would repeat: the reason `rawVcard` is an S0b blocker (§4.2.1). ⭐ *Since contacts v2 ([`contacts-app.md`](contacts-app.md) §9.10) only a pre-v2 row or a fenced v1 peer's push can be one, and it lands small once a device moves it; `ContactPhotoRowMaxSharedReplicaTest` pins both halves on the simulator* | the WAL stays under `Wmax + δ` |
| F7 | A sibling wipes (Control's device-forget) | §5.1 | next access: epoch differs and `meta.wipe` is there → fenced `UPDATING` → "Refreshing…" while the wipe runs (this app may resume it, §6); the last chunk's epoch → `REPLACED`'s step 4: the probe, then rebuild or deprovision, in the foreground. An app whose first access comes after the last chunk sees `REPLACED` directly |
| F8 | A newer sibling migrates while an older one runs | §5.2 | older: epoch differs → versions above → fenced `SKEW` → update surface |
| F9 | An older app launches on a newer store | open: versions above → `ROLLBACK` | nothing; the store is untouched |
| F9b | An older app opens a store of a newer `meta.layout` whose DDL its own `CREATE` statements would fail on | step 2 reads the marker only; step 3 finds the layout above: `ROLLBACK`, `SKEW`, handle released. No DDL ran | nothing |
| F9c | A crash after the fresh store's commit, before the WAL switch | the next open sets and reads back WAL before anything else (§2.3.1) | nothing; until then no connection used the store |
| F9d | WAL cannot be entered or does not read back | `StoreUnusable`, logged, "storage unavailable", handle released | nothing |
| F9e | The app is backgrounded or a wake expires during a migration or a wipe | **migration**: the run stops after its last committed chunk; a chunk in flight is interrupted and rolled back; the marker, its epoch, `migration_done` and the committed chunks stay. **Wipe** (always chunked, §5.1): the same: the chunk in flight is interrupted and rolled back; `meta.wipe`, its epoch and the committed chunks stay; **a wipe call in progress throws `WipeNotFinished`, so its caller reports no success and purges no custody** (§5.1) | **updating**, resumed on a `REPLACEMENT` handle by the next qualifying open (§5.2 step 2: a migration in the foreground; a wipe in the foreground or in a wake under its token) |
| F9f | A peer deletes a row this process listens on | catch-up fires one absence notification; `DatabaseImpl` empties the snapshot and fires `onReset` | — (this process: the stream re-reads and shows the deletion) |
| F9g | A current-version store that keeps the marker but lacks a table (e.g. `objects`) or an index | the schema validation of §5.2 finds the mismatch: fenced `CORRUPT`, preserved, surfaced; no `CREATE IF NOT EXISTS` | nothing |
| F9h | An older app is the only client of a newer WAL store with frames | classified through a read-only connection: `SKEW`, released; or, if the read-only open cannot initialise the `-shm`, `StoreUnclassifiable`. No read/write connection is ever opened | the newer store's `objects.db` and `-wal` unchanged, no checkpoint; its `-shm` possibly rebuilt, which the newer build revalidates at its next read |
| F10 | Open before first unlock | `ProtectedDataUnavailable` | nothing; the wake exits (`finished = false`) |
| F11 | A background launch finds a store needing migration | `StoreNeedsForeground`, nothing written | nothing |
| F12 | The file is corrupt (a CORRUPT row of §5.2.2) | classified at step 2, or met by an access, with no write and no persistent pragma; the detecting process writes `replica/CORRUPT`; fenced `CORRUPT`, handle released (S18); Control runs the writer drain and waits `CKPT_MAX` for any checkpoint already running, then takes one consistent snapshot (`VACUUM INTO`, else the backup API, else a byte copy verified by fingerprint and retried up to 3 times, else none, and says so) and offers an export only of a verified one; the "Storage damaged" surface states the unsynced-data risk (§6); no automatic delete or replace (S1) | each process finds the same at its next access. Recovery is D8 |
| F12b | A sibling that never touches the damaged pages is committing when corruption is detected elsewhere | its next outermost access finds `replica/CORRUPT` at step 0 inside the write lock and fences itself; a transaction it began before the marker finished before Control's writer drain returned, so it is in the snapshot; **a checkpoint it began before the marker ends within `CKPT_MAX`, which Control waits out, and none begins after** | no commit and no new checkpoint after the marker; a byte copy that a checkpoint still touched fails its fingerprint check and is discarded, never offered (S20) |
| F12c | Power is lost right after corruption was detected | the marker was reported only after its rename and the directory sync, so it survives; a marker whose write had not finished leaves at most a temporary file, and the next access that meets the corruption writes it again | every process still fences at its next access |
| F12d | The `-wal` is damaged (header or a frame overwritten, or cut short) by the medium or the file system, with commits in it not yet checkpointed | **nothing is detected by SQLite**: every open succeeds, `quick_check` is `ok`, no marker (§5.2.2's last row; *Q0, simulator*, results doc §11 (4)). The commits after the damaged point are gone. If one of them had raised `meta.hlc_watermark` for a tip **any app on this store** published, the lost-commit check logs a typed diagnostic (§5.4): it compares `meta` with the maximum over every app's identity-bound item, at open and again in the publish transaction before `meta` is raised, so whichever app comes first reports it and no publish heals `meta` unreported; nothing else happens: no fence, no cursor change | accepted residual R5: local writes that had not synced are lost. Synced data can be re-pulled once the recovery is specified and built; until then the loss is detected and logged, and the device stays behind until its next full resync by other means (a wipe of the store, §5.1) |
| F13 | Two apps create the store at once | both find `objects.db` absent; one `O_EXCL` creation wins, the other gets `EEXIST`; both classify the empty file fresh read-only; the first creates it under `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`; the second's `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` waits, then its re-read (§5.2 step 2a) finds an existing store and judges it, running no `CREATE` | consistent; verified in Q0 |
| F14 | The connection was closed by quiesce; the app resumes | the still-registered handle reopens through the registry on its first admitted access; read `meta` unconditionally | — (this process: keeps its cache if `(epoch, seq)` unchanged) |
| F15 | A statement left un-reset (a bug) | the exit assertion throws in tests, logs in production; quiesce's close finalizes it | the WAL cannot be checkpointed past it until then (*GK*) |

## 12. Walks for the cases the draft's rounds raised

| # | Raised in the draft as | Now | Holds |
|---|---|---|---|
| W1 | Saving from a stale cache over a sibling's rows (Split View, a wake during use) | B's save is an access: `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`, `data_version` moved, `seq` moved, cache dropped, block reads current rows, writes, commits | S3, S4 |
| W2 | A cancel committing between reading the row and acquiring the lease | one transaction holds the write lock across both; the cancel's `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` waits | S15 |
| W3 | Crash after advancing the generation / mid-transaction / a torn generation write | there is no separate generation; F1/F2 | S9 |
| W4 | A wipe that only advanced the generation left holders able to write (a sync cycle writing a cursor past wiped rows) | the wipe moves the epoch; the holder's next access is fenced and throws on write | S11 |
| W5 | A wipe under one hold breaking the 1 s ceiling (finding 2) | no wipe is one hold: every wipe is budgeted chunks, each under 1 s and interruptible, behind `meta.wipe` (§5.1, D13) | S8, S9, S21 |
| W6 | A fenced runtime with no way back (finding 3), and an orphaned graph keeping its connection (round 2) | §6: `replaced` → host → "Refreshing…" → stop the graph → release the handle through the registry → orphan the graph → rebuild in the foreground with a new registered handle. A quiesce in between closes the runtime handle's connection and keeps it registered until the fence releases it (job handles are released at quiesce, §2.8) | S11, S18 |
| W7 | A wake expiring in the foreground stopped the session (finding 1) | its token ends; `protected` stays true; nothing else changes | S6 |
| W8 | A thread waiting for the lock when the app expires | between slices it holds nothing and is not counted; within a slice, `closeAndDrain` waits ≤ 50 ms; if it then obtains the lock with the gate closed, it rolls back at once | S5, S7 |
| W9 | The lock file or generation file deleted behind a running process | nothing in the design deletes a store file (S1); a tool that does is outside it, and F12 is where a damaged file lands | S1 |
| W10 | The store-less wipe leaving a live store's memory believing in rows | one wipe function; the live store's handle sees the new epoch at its next access (or runs the wipe itself, and then clears its resident state and fences itself before the commit returns) | S4, S11, S17 |
| W11 | An older build deleting what a newer one migrated (M12) | the older build refuses; the newer one's migration fences it, from the chain's Start (a chunked migration, "updating") as after its Finish | S12 |
| W12 | `open` migrating under a sibling, unlocked | the open is a read-only classification and a gated write transaction; the sibling is fenced by the epoch | S2, S11, S12, S19 |

## 13. Phases

Each phase leaves master working and has a device step that the person with the iPhone can run.
⚠⚠ **Rule, so that it does: the caller changes for an unfinished wipe land in the same change that
first makes the chunked store reachable from a forget or wipe caller, never later.** Those changes
are §5.1's steps 3 and 4: `ForgetThisDeviceImplementation` and `ControlSurface.wipeDeviceState`
tell `WipeNotFinished` apart from "not dropped", stop before the custody purge and report "not
finished", and `forgetThisDevice(storeWiped = true)` skips its cursor write. Without them an
interrupted chunked wipe is folded into an ordinary miss and custody is purged over a store still
behind `meta.wipe`, the custody-gone, store-present state D3 forbids. **The store becomes reachable
when it is bound in place of `openFileObjectStore`, which is S0b-1's last slice**, so they are
S0b-1's. S0b-1's earlier slices (the driver, then the store core, the one being built first) are
bound into no app: until the binding lands, no forget path can reach the chunked wipe.
⚠⚠ Until **S0b-4**, no App Group build is to be installed for these phases (⚠ App Group builds of
the real apps are nevertheless on the maintainer's iPhone as of 2026-10-06, and are being killed
with `0xdead10cc`; accepted until S0b ships, §4.1): the device steps of Q0 to S0b-3 use the
benchmark app (`spike-ios-store/`, then still installed, *Spike* §7; the module was deleted on
2026-11-05, last version at `066f6f363`) extended into **two apps on a
separate group** (`group.app.tenshu.storebench`), so they never touch the product container.

| Phase | What | Gate | Device step |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Q0** | **Measure what the spike could not.** Two bench apps on the bench group, the minimal SQLite store with §2.3's settings. Fix the spike's two harness gaps first (a failed launch or phase fails the run; `mincore`/`msync` return codes checked). | — | ⭐ **Gate zero PASSED on the phone, 2026-10-04**: every point, the interrupt latencies and the re-measured spike are in [`ios-shared-store-sqlite-q0-results.md`](ios-shared-store-sqlite-q0-results.md). ⭐ **The simulator half of (a) to (ad) and the soak ran on 2026-10-05, with nothing launched on the phone:** the results doc sorts every item into simulator-answered (§8 there), device-only (§9 there, with the commands and an inventory of which have since run on the phone and which are pending), or not measurable until S0b code exists (§10). **Read its §11 first: it is where the run contradicts this design**, above all that `sqlite3_interrupt` does not reach the one-shot wipe and that `N_time`'s basis is wrong. ⭐ **Both were settled on 2026-10-06 by removing the one-shot wipe: every wipe is chunked (D13, §5.1)**; the cold device figures behind that are the results doc's §13. Ship gate (t)'s fact holds on the simulator (an interrupt reaches a checkpoint while it copies frames, every time); (j) was proven in gate zero. **No placeholder is replaced: none has a device-measured value yet.** Of the two harness gaps, the failed-launch one is fixed; the `mincore`/`msync` return codes are not, and `evict` is now refused on a device (results doc §5). ⚠⚠ **(0) Gate zero, before anything else is measured: the driver route, end to end on the device** (§2.1.1). The bench app, built with the store's own thin driver and **the vendored SQLite build of §2.1.2** (D12), with no `androidx.sqlite` artifact on its iOS classpath: **first, `sqlite3_libversion_number()` is at or above 3.51.3 (or a fixed backport) and the driver refuses to open on the androidx 3.50.1 binary**; it links exactly one SQLite (`sqlite3_sourceid()` is the vendored build's); opens with `sqlite3_open_v2` and holds the `sqlite3*`; sets `SQLITE_DBCONFIG_NO_CKPT_ON_CLOSE` and reads it back as on; closes the last connection with frames in the WAL and finds the `-wal` untouched; and **interrupts a running statement from another thread** with `sqlite3_interrupt` on that handle, the statement returning `SQLITE_INTERRUPT`. **If the handle cannot be reached, or either call does not take effect, nothing else in this design holds: Q0 stops here and S0b is redesigned.** Then **re-measure the spike** (point reads, single-row commits, the 150k-row wipe, the type scan) on this build: it is a different SQLite version with a different option set, so the spike's numbers are indicative until this run replaces them. And, since the bug this guards against is a race: two processes committing while a third checkpoints and rewinds in a loop, for an hour, followed by `PRAGMA integrity_check` (a soak, not a proof; the proof is the version). (a) A writes 1,000 single rows, B observes each with `data_version` and `meta.seq` across **processes**. (b) **Termination rule:** A holds `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` and is backgrounded with no assertion → expect a `0xdead10cc` report (`devicectl … --domain-type systemCrashLogs`). (c) A backgrounded with an **idle open WAL connection** → record whether it is killed (informational: every connection is closed at quiesce). (d) Wipe at 150k across processes; B fenced at its next access. (e) Cost of an empty `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`/`COMMIT`. (f) Both apps creating the store at once, ×20. (g) Flash-cold reads after a reboot (the spike's open item). (h) Read back the protection class and backup flag on `replica/`, `-wal`, `-shm`. (i) Time a checkpoint (`PASSIVE`, and `RESTART` with no reader) against WAL size, cold and warm, to set `T` and, with (s), `Wmax` by the 200 ms p99 rule. (j) **Ship requirement** (first proven in gate zero): close-time checkpointing is suppressed with `SQLITE_DBCONFIG_NO_CKPT_ON_CLOSE` on every connection kind the store's driver opens (read/write, read-only, a second connection in the process); closing the last connection then leaves `-wal` untouched. (o) `backgroundTimeRemaining` right after backgrounding and inside each wake type, for the admission checks of §4.2.1's operations table. (k) That a connection the store's driver opens with `SQLITE_OPEN_READONLY` cannot write, that closing such a connection leaves `objects.db` and `-wal` unchanged and runs no checkpoint, and what its open returns as the first connection to a WAL file with frames. (l) The cost of the per-access `stat` of `replica/CORRUPT`, and that a sibling which never reads the damaged pages fences itself at its next access. (m) The time of `PRAGMA quick_check` against `page_count` at several sizes, to set its size bound at 1 s (it holds a read mark throughout). (k′) That a read-only open of a zero-length `objects.db` classifies as an empty database. (p) That `wal_checkpoint(RESTART)` on the `CHECKPOINT` connection, with a sibling holding a read mark, returns busy within each 50 ms slice and succeeds once the reader ends; that after it the next write restarts the log and the `-wal` is truncated to at most `Wmax/4`; that a `PASSIVE` checkpoint with a reader present leaves the rewind write appending (the case the ceiling must defer); the p99 time a read mark is held by an ordinary access, to set `B_ckpt`; and the checkpoint's time against `w`. (q) That `F_FULLFSYNC` on the `replica/` directory descriptor is accepted on the device, else `fsync`. (r) An older build's read-only classification of a newer store with frames in its WAL and `-shm` deleted: `objects.db` and `-wal` hash identical before and after; then the newer build opens cleanly and reads every frame. (s) The WAL-index rebuild time against `-wal` size (first open after every connection closed), separately from checkpoint time, to set `R` and `Wmax`; and that the rewind write rewinds and truncates the `-wal` to `journal_size_limit` after a full backfill, and that the file never shrinks otherwise, so that step 4's size check (back at or below `Wmax − δ`) is a sound proof of the reset. (u) **The wipe's chunks** (as a model here, the real wipe in S0b-1): a chunk's time and its WAL against `Wmax`, and the whole wipe's duration at several store sizes, a typical 150,000-row store included, which is what the user waits through (§5.1's accepted cost; 38 to 45 ms a 1,000-row chunk at p50 on the phone so far, results doc §13.1); and `V(n)` for `incremental_vacuum` at several `n`, to set `n_time`. ⚠ *Measured, and no longer an input:* the removed one-shot `DELETE FROM objects`' WAL growth and its time against `page_count` (20,000 to 250,000 pages, cold and warm). It set no switch in the end: it is the evidence for D13 (uninterruptible; about 14 µs per page uncached), and it stays useful only as the phone's uncached page-read rate, which also sizes `quick_check`'s bound (m). (v) A chunked migration of a service holding most of a 150k-row store, with a row whose hash is the smallest present and one at `Long.MIN_VALUE`: chunk times, WAL never above `Wmax`, a kill mid-run, a resume that finishes with no row skipped or migrated twice, and the verification count at 0, with a test whose budget cuts a page short; and the time of the verification's counting statement at 150k rows. (w) The largest encoded row in the real store on the iPhone (today's app-local file stores: the largest `.obj` file per app), by type, against `ROW_MAX`. (x) That `wal + C + h` upper-bounds the real WAL growth of every statement (the `-wal` size before and after each statement and after `COMMIT`) across inserts, rewrites of large rows, and hash-ordered and random deletes; the typical pages per write; and the B-tree fill assumption behind the depths in `G`'s derivation (page fill from `dbstat` if the bundled build has it, else depth by `PRAGMA` page walks). (z) The p99 of a `COMMIT` sync at `synchronous=FULL` (`S`) and of `F_FULLFSYNC` on a small file and a directory (`S_full`), in protected background time, for §4.2.1's admissions. (ab) **With `cache_size = C`, does the `-wal` file size after each statement track the pages the transaction has dirtied to within `C`** (plus the statement's pinned pages)? Across a transaction that dirties many more than `C` pages with no cache miss, one that rewrites `ROW_MAX` rows, and one rolled back; that a spill in WAL mode takes no further lock and a concurrent reader in another process sees nothing of it; that a rolled-back transaction's spilled frames are overwritten by the next one rather than accumulating; and the read latencies of §3.3 and the spike at `cache_size = C` against the default. If the size does not track, the summed formula returns, with a pointer-map allowance per balancing page and overflow terms for the lease's table and index. (ad) **The corrupt-store snapshot:** that `BEGIN EXCLUSIVE` in WAL mode does not stop a sibling's `PASSIVE` checkpoint (the reason the design does not rely on it); that a sibling refuses every checkpoint path once `replica/CORRUPT` exists; that a checkpoint started just before the marker ends within `CKPT_MAX`; that the fingerprint (sizes, modification times, the three hashes) changes when a sibling checkpoints during a byte copy and is stable when nothing runs; and `sqlite3_backup` on a store with a damaged B-tree page (it completes) and with a damaged header (it fails, and the byte copy runs). (ac) **The hold watchdog and `ROW_MAX`'s time bound:** the p99, cold, of a `ROW_MAX` insert and of a `ROW_MAX`-over-`ROW_MAX` rewrite (if either is near `HOLD_MAX`, `ROW_MAX` comes down); the latency from `sqlite3_interrupt` to the statement returning, during such a rewrite, during a multi-row `DELETE` and during `quick_check`; that an interrupt with no statement running affects nothing later; and the p99 duration of ordinary transactions in a real session against `HOLD_MAX`. (aa) The time of the publish's batched `SecItemCopyMatching` (`kSecMatchLimitAll` over ten per-app items, data returned, or the `kSecAttrGeneric` fallback if data is refused with that limit) and of one `SecItemUpdate` / `SecItemAdd` in the shared access group, both outside the SQLite lock. (y) The largest relation array (`TList` row) and its member count in the real stores, the iPhone's app-local stores and the Android and desktop `objects.db`, and the WAL one enqueue costs at that size. (t) **Ship gate:** `sqlite3_interrupt`, called from another thread through the store's own cinterop, reaches a running checkpoint (`PASSIVE` and `RESTART`) and returns within a measured bound; if not, the cap of §4.2.1 applies and needs the user's sign-off. |

## 14. Decisions

⭐ **D1–D10 accepted as recommended, 2026-10-03** (maintainer); **D11 and D12 decided by the user, 2026-10-04; D13 decided by the user, 2026-10-06** (it changes D11's wipe clause). The *Recommendation* column is the
decision. D9 was revised in review after that acceptance (§5.4) and ⭐ **re-confirmed in its revised
wording, 2026-10-03.**

| **D1** | Module placement | (a) drop `iosX64` from `:core-common`; (b) `iosSqliteMain` source set in `:core-common`; (c) a new module | **(b)**, falling back to (c) if it does not compile (§2.1). **Implementation refinement, found in review (not a new product decision):** the store does not use `BundledSQLiteDriver`, which gives out no `sqlite3*`; it uses its own thin driver, owning the handle (§2.1.1). **And the SQLite binary is not androidx's** (3.50.1 in every release so far, which has the WAL-reset bug): the store builds its own, by D12 (§2.1.2) |
| **D2** | `synchronous` | `NORMAL`; `FULL`; `FULL` + `fullfsync` | **`FULL`**: the file store's durability class at ~1/15 its cost (§2.3) |

| **D4** | `transaction { }` on exception | commit what was written (today); roll back | **commit**: same meaning on every platform; crash atomicity is gained either way (§2.5) |

If Q0 (j) fails, the App Group build does not ship and S0b needs a redesign (§4.2.1). Q0 (c) is informational. Refined in review, unchanged in substance: the runtime handle's connection is closed and the handle kept; every short-lived job handle is released (§2.8's table) |

Splitting the wire is the escalation** (§5.4, §8). Accepted 2026-10-03 as "keep the file"; changed in review  ⭐ **Amended, approved by the user 2026-10-04:** plus an identity-bound copy in the shared Keychain group, in the same `(ownerId, deviceId)`-bound frame, never read unbound; **implemented as one item per app** (each written only by its own app, the copy's value the maximum over the bound items), read before and raised after the SQLite transaction that publishes a tip, never inside it, and always raised before the tip is sent (an implementation of the approved copy, not a new decision); **the floor is the maximum of both homes, everywhere**, so deleting every app keeps it too; a tip that cannot be persisted is not published (§5.4). |
