| **D11** ⭐ **decided by the user, 2026-10-04** | How every WAL-index recovery and checkpoint is bounded | per-open size checks (each could go stale); a last-closer rule (unbounded after a crash); a sidecar lock serialising opens with large writers; **a WAL ceiling `Wmax` enforced by writers** | **A WAL ceiling `Wmax` enforced by writers (S21): migrations become resumable chunks behind a fenced "updating" state (§5.3); wipes stay one transaction, as one truncate-optimised `DELETE` (§5.1).** ⚠ Refined in review: a wipe stays one transaction only while its WAL estimate from `page_count` fits in `δ` (up to ~1.8 GiB at the current `δ`) **and its time fits the hold ceiling (`page_count ≤ N_time`, about 137 MiB at the placeholder, which is the bound that binds)**; past that it runs as budgeted chunks behind the same fence as a migration, the user's accepted cost applying to it too. ⚠⚠ **Amended 2026-10-06 by D13: the wipe clause above no longer holds. Every wipe is chunked and no wipe is one transaction**; the rest of D11 stands. The user's rationale: the bound becomes structural, every open and every checkpoint costs at most a constant, with no check to go stale; and a large migration no longer runs in one transaction on the launch path, which removes the ~20 s launch-watchdog risk. The cost, accepted: siblings are locked out during a migration, and after a crash mid-migration until a compatible build resumes it |

Pulling in other dependencies does not sound helpful for me for a small wrapper."** The vendored amalgamation at or above 3.51.3, built for `iosArm64` and `iosSimulatorArm64`, with the project's own cinterop over the vendored `sqlite3.h`; **no `androidx.sqlite` artifact on iOS**, neither the binary, nor the published declarations, nor the interfaces (nothing in shared code needs them, §2.1). (B) and (C) rejected. Cost: a vendored `sqlite3.c`, one build task per iOS target, and re-measuring the spike in Q0 |
| **D13** ⭐ **decided by the user, 2026-10-06** | How the store wipes itself (changes D11's wipe clause) | (a) one-shot below a size and time switch (`page_count ≤ N_time`, the WAL estimate inside `δ`), chunked above it (D11 as refined); **(b) every wipe chunked, the one-shot wipe removed** | **(b).** Asked whether to use the chunked behaviour for every wipe and remove the one-step version, the maintainer answered: *"Yes, sounds good please implement it"*. **Why:** the one-shot `DELETE FROM objects` cannot be interrupted (0 of 42 attempts on the simulator, 0 of 6 on the iPhone: `OP_Clear` has no interrupt check), and its time is the time to read every page it frees: 0.4 to 0.9 µs per page cached, about 14 µs per page uncached on the iPhone (cold after a reboot, 2026-10-05: 284 ms at 20,158 pages, 717 ms at 50,130, 1,437 ms at 100,068, 5,526 ms at 250,099; results doc §11 (1), (2), §13.1). An uncached wipe would hold the shared write lock for seconds with no way to stop it, breaking S8's 1 s ceiling and risking the suspended-lock termination; the switch guarding it could not be set safely for a busy disk. The chunked wipe on the same phone: 38 to 45 ms per 1,000-row chunk at p50, 56 ms at worst, the WAL inside `Wmax`. **The cost, accepted:** every wipe, even of a small store, is a resumable job; siblings show "Refreshing…" while it runs; a kill mid-wipe leaves the store marked until a compatible build resumes it (a wake may); the wipe call returns only after the last chunk (`WipeableObjectStore.kt:33-35`), so a forget waits for it and one interrupted mid-wipe must be repeated by the user; a wipe takes seconds rather than milliseconds (§5.1, §15.1 R3). `N_time`, the `page_count` admission and the `K` estimate are retired (§5.1 keeps them once, as history) |
| **D14** ⭐ **decided by the maintainer, 2026-10-19** ("delete the files, then purge") | A deprovision whose wipe is refused because the store can **never** be wiped (`Corrupt`, or `Skew`: written by a newer build), between RG-3's D3 (no store left behind custody's purge) and A4 (no custody at rest once Control cleared the bridge) | keep custody until the store is wiped (A4 broken for good on such a store); purge and leave the store (D3 broken); **delete the store's files, then purge** | **Delete the files, then purge** (Appendix B.13 (179)): only when SQLite proves that no connection is open on the store anywhere (leaving WAL succeeds), under the exclusive lock, so no connection is left on deleted files; a busy store keeps custody and the next deprovision tries again. It satisfies both, and A4's promise is kept, not changed |

## 15. Not known, deferred, or contradicted

### 15.1 ⚠⚠ Accepted residuals needing the user's sign-off before ship

One list; nothing outside it is an accepted residual.

| # | Residual | When it bites | What bounds it |
|---|---|---|---|
| **R1** | An uninterruptible call (a checkpoint, an open's index rebuild) outlives its token if Q0 (t) shows `sqlite3_interrupt` cannot reach it. ⭐ *Q0, simulator:* it **does** reach a running checkpoint, `PASSIVE` and `RESTART`, every time it arrived while frames were being copied (96 of 96 in the last four runs, results doc §8.6); one that arrives in the final sync does not, which is R2; the bound is still the phone's to measure. The same run found a call R1 did not name, the one-shot wipe's uninterruptible `DELETE` (results doc §11 (1), (2)); ⭐ **D13 removed that statement (2026-10-06), so it is not a residual** | only if Q0 (t) fails on the phone | `Wmax` sized so the p99 of `R + T` is 200 ms, a 20× headroom on the 2 s margin (§4.2.1) |
| **R2** | An `fsync` slower than its p99 plus the 2 s margin: a `COMMIT`'s sync, a checkpoint's final sync, a marker's `F_FULLFSYNC`. No hard stop exists once it has started, **and the hold watchdog stops at it**: S8's 1 s ceiling is enforced up to the commit sync, and the sync's own duration is this residual | a pathological flash stall, in protected background time (the token) or at any time (the hold a sibling waits on) | admission on `remaining` (§4.2.1's operations table), Q0 (z) |
| **R3** ⭐ **accepted by the user with D13, 2026-10-06** | **Every wipe is a resumable chunked job behind a fence** (§5.1), a store of any size, where an earlier revision chunked only a store past a size switch. So: (1) the wipe call returns only after the last chunk, so the caller ("Forget this device", Control's discard) waits those seconds, and **a forget interrupted mid-wipe is not completed by the wipe's resumer**: the store is emptied, custody is not purged, the device keeps its identity with its row already retired at the relay, and the user repeats the forget, which completes in every case (§5.1 traces the half-state: an A1 holder that is only reopened re-admits itself, a joiner stays fenced; that seconds-wide window is accepted too, 2026-10-06, follow-ups in `tech-debt.md`); a kill or crash mid-wipe leaves the store marked, and **every app is locked out** ("Refreshing…") until the next open of a build that does not judge the store newer resumes it on a `REPLACEMENT` handle (§5.2), which a background wake may do; (2) siblings show "Refreshing…" for the whole wipe, not for one transaction; (3) a wipe takes seconds, not milliseconds: 38 to 45 ms per 1,000-row chunk at p50 on the iPhone 17e, about 41 to 49 s for a 1,058,632-row store (*Q0, device, as a model*, results doc §13.1), and roughly 6 to 7 s for a typical 150,000-row store, ⚠ **an extrapolation until S0b-1 measures the real wipe** | every wipe: "Forget this device", Control's discard path, a below-floor wipe at open | each chunk under 1 s and `TX_BUDGET`, interruptible (S8, S21); resumable by any qualifying build, in the foreground or in a wake (S13); the same accepted cost as a migration (D11). What it buys: no wipe holds the shared write lock uninterruptibly (the removed one-shot `DELETE` took 1.4 s at 391 MiB and 5.5 s at 977 MiB uncached on the phone, results doc §13.1) |
| **R4** ⭐ **accepted by the user, 2026-10-04, as pre-existing and out of S0b's scope** | **Cross-app tip ordering.** Each publish computes a tip at or above every tip already published (§5.4), but two apps sharing the identity send independently: A computes a lower tip and pauses, B computes and sends a higher one, A sends. The relay keeps the last arrival (`HlcTipStore.record`, "even if it regressed"; `SqliteHlcTipStore.kt:23-24`, `ON CONFLICT … DO UPDATE SET tip = excluded.tip`; *Read*), so the slot steps back. **Pre-existing:** today every route-1 app runs its own `SyncScheduler` under the shared identity, and `buildSignedTip` raises the watermark, signs and sends outside any lock (`SyncScheduler.kt:2398-2443`, *Read*); within one process `tickMutex` serialises it (`:429`, `:722`). Probably also web tabs sharing one identity, and shared-realm tips (`buildSharedTip`) (*inferred*, not traced) | two apps publishing within one request's latency of each other (Split View, a wake beside the foreground app) | **transient:** peers show a false `DIVERGENCE` until the next higher tip lands; **GC-safe:** a lower slot only delays tombstone GC. ⭐ **Decided follow-up, its own PR, merged only on the user's word:** a relay-side monotonic slot, `max(stored, incoming)` per `(ownerId, deviceId)`, plus a relay log line and a response signal whenever an incoming tip regresses, so the T-T-04 diagnostic intent of `sync-hlc-tip-device-identity.md` D2 survives; with an amendment to that D2, a threat-model amendment (House Rule 2) and a `RELAY_PROTOCOL_VERSION` assessment. Holding the SQLite lock across the send is ruled out (network I/O under the lock); a single publisher via the scheduler lease was considered and set aside (it would extend the lease to the foreground loop, iOS only) |
| **R5** ⭐ **accepted by the user, 2026-10-06** (*"Lets just accept both for now"*) | **A damaged `-wal` loses commits with no verdict** (*Q0, simulator*, results doc §11 (4)). With the log's header or a frame overwritten, or the file cut short, every open succeeds, `quick_check` says `ok`, `VACUUM INTO` and the backup complete, and the commits after the damaged point are gone (200 of 200, or 98 of 200, in the run). It is how SQLite reads a WAL: the log ends at the first frame whose checksum fails. **What is lost:** every commit since the last complete checkpoint that lies after the damage. **Local writes that had not synced are gone.** Rows that had already synced are still on the relay and can be re-pulled **once the recovery is specified and built** (§5.4's open item); until then the loss is detected and logged, and the device stays behind until its next full resync by other means (a wipe of the store, §5.1). **Nothing repairs it:** the frames are not there to replay, and SQLite reports nothing to act on. **Rejected:** a per-commit counter in a sidecar file, to detect every such loss: it costs a sync on every commit, and it still recovers nothing | damage to the medium or the file system under the `-wal`, **not a crash** (with `synchronous=FULL` a crash only drops a write that was never confirmed) | the window is at most the WAL since the last complete checkpoint, itself at most `Wmax + δ` (S21). **Detection, built in S0b-1:** the lost-commit check at open (§5.4): `meta.hlc_watermark` below the maximum over every app's identity-bound Keychain item, compared at open and again before any publish raises `meta`, is logged as a typed diagnostic, **and that is all S0b-1 does**; it sees only a loss that crossed a published tip. Recovery (rewinding cursors so the app pulls again) is a named open design item (§5.4, F12d) |

The outcome of R1 and R2 is a terminated app (`0xdead10cc`), which frees its locks; the store is left
as of its last commit (S9).

- ⚠⚠ **Pre-existing exposure to the WAL-reset bug, elsewhere in the repo** (found while fixing it for

Which deployments can do that is **not traced** |
  | The sync relay (`RelayDatabase`) | `org.xerial:sqlite-jdbc` 3.53.4.0 (`sync-relay-server/build.gradle.kts:49`), SQLite 3.53.4 by that artifact's version scheme (*inferred*): above the fix | **one** connection behind a lock (`RelayDatabase.kt:24-40`) | no, twice over |
  | Commerce | not SQLite: a pooled JDBC database (`commerce-service/build.gradle.kts:55` contrasts it with "the relay's single-connection SQLite") | — | no |
  | Web | IndexedDB, not SQLite | — | no |
  | `spike-ios-store` | androidx 2.7.1, 3.50.1 | one process, one connection at a time (*Spike*) | no; a bench, not shipped (deleted 2026-11-05, last version at `066f6f363`) |

- **Not measured, and built on anyway:** two processes, the App Group container, the termination
  rule for SQLite's locks, flash-cold device reads, an empty
  `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`/`COMMIT`, a production-shaped store under real services (*Spike* §6). Q0 measures
  the first five before S0b-1 is reviewed as final.
- **Deferred, with triggers:** a `DEFERRED` read path on a second connection (trigger: S0b-4 step (e)
  shows readers waiting on writers); a change-sequence column for incremental catch-up (trigger: the
  same step shows refills hurting); nothing else.
- **Not traced:** whether the callers of `SchemaDrivenContentWalk.pagesOf` and `decodeRow` hold
  `DatabaseLock` (§2.5 makes it moot on iOS, not on the JVM); where the inference embedding store
  lives on iOS (lease draft §3.2 note 2).
- ⚠ **Pre-existing, found while specifying forget, not caused by S0b** (*Read*):
  1. The shared `ForgetThisDevice` operation clears no cross-app custody on iOS: it wipes the store
     and calls `SyncManager.forgetThisDevice()` (`ForgetThisDeviceImplementation.kt:78-81`), and
     `RealmKeyMaterialBridge.clear()` is reached only through `ControlSurface.clearDriveSession()`
     (`ControlSurface.kt:1208-1211`), whose callers are `wipeDeviceState` (`:1473`) and
     `ControlIosApp.swift:563` (the `-clearDriveSession` debug probe). **Exposure today:** no Swift caller of the operation was found; the iOS
     UI uses `wipeDeviceState`, which does clear the bridge. Whether any client can invoke the
     operation on iOS (its permission entry) was not traced. If one can, the siblings keep adopting a
     forgotten identity.
  2. ⭐ **Fixed on master since (`wipeDeviceState` now clears the bridge first, `ControlSurface.kt:1426-1434`).** As found: `wipeDeviceState` cleared the bridge **last**, after the store and Control's custody, and running
     siblings learn of it only at their next launch or foreground probe (`ControlSurface.kt:1201-1204`
     says so). **Exposure today:** yes, on any device with siblings running when Control forgets;
     bounded because the retired device's tokens stop verifying at the relay. With S0b's shared store
     the window would widen into a re-adoption at rebuild, which is why §5.1 moves the clear first.
- ⚠ **Pre-existing, found while tying the watermark copy to publication:** the shared-realm tip
  (`buildSharedTip`, `SyncScheduler.kt:1822-1835`) merges through no watermark at all; it signs the
  realm processor's in-process clock. So a shared realm's slot still sees the restart and
  multi-runtime backward steps the personal watermark fixed (the tip doc's C1, C3). Not S0b's to fix;
  the publish sequence applies to the personal tip only. Its cross-app send order is R4's race too,
  which R4's relay follow-up closes for every slot.
- ⚠ **Pre-existing: cross-app tip ordering** (§15.1 R4). The watermark makes every *computed* tip
  monotone; it cannot order two processes' requests at the relay, which records the last arrival.
  Today's code has the same race on iOS route-1 (`SyncScheduler.kt:2398-2443`). Transient, GC-safe,
  out of S0b's scope; the decided fix is the relay-side monotonic slot of R4.
- **Contradicted:** the JVM `SqliteObjectStore` comments claim a `type` index its schema does not
  create (`:402`, `:432` against `:1227-1232`); T-C-04 says iOS app storage is excluded from backup,
  and no code sets the flag on the replica (§2.4); `ios-background-scheduling.md` §4.1.1 said the
  lease draft was open and not on master (it was merged as a draft; corrected with this
  document).
- **Nothing found that contradicts the spike's numbers.** One caution on reading them: the spike's
  SQLite store had no row cache and no transaction per access, so its point-read figures are a
  floor for this design's cache misses and a ceiling for its hits, and the per-access transaction
  cost is new and unmeasured (Q0 (e)).
- **Against the draft:** its §15.2 listed what SQLite would not remove as the suspended-lock rule,
  M12 and the lease. All three stay, but the lease gets simpler (§9.2) and M12 cheaper (§7); and the
  draft's "the store lock is held for reads too" property is preserved deliberately (§2.5), so S0b
  does not yet take SQLite's non-blocking readers.

## Appendix A. Threat-model amendment text (lands with S0b-4's code, not before)

⭐ **Landed in S0b-4 slice 2 (B.21, 2026-11-01), amended to what is built** (B.21.2 (365)): T-T-08's
identity-bound watermark in `meta` (§5.4) is not built, so the landed text says the watermark is
still `sync-hlc/` and that the cutover removes it with the old store; A5 and T-C-04 say "on a build
with the shared store switched on". `threat-model.md` is the text that holds; the drafts below are
kept as drafted.

**A5, appended after the C4e amendment:**

> *Amendment (iOS shared replica on SQLite, [`ios-shared-store-sqlite.md`](../proposals/ios-shared-store-sqlite.md)):*
> on iOS the route-1 shared replica moves from the one-file-per-object `FileObjectStore` to a single
> SQLite database, `replica/objects.db` (with SQLite's `-wal` and `-shm`), in the same App-Group
> container (`group.app.tenshu.shared`). The rows are the same `DbEntryCodec` plaintext as before
> (A5 user data + A6 metadata at rest, decodable without key material). **Write integrity** now rests
> on SQLite's own locking and transactions instead of the advisory `flock`: every store access is
> one SQLite transaction holding the database write lock, a multi-row change is atomic against a
> crash, and a sibling never observes part of one; a replacement of the store (a wipe, a migration)
> moves a random epoch that fences every other process's handle before it can write. As before, the
> lock is an integrity discipline among trusted first-party writers, not a confidentiality boundary.
> **At rest:** the `replica/` directory is set explicitly to
> `NSFileProtectionCompleteUntilFirstUserAuthentication` (previously the unasserted default) and
> excluded from backup (`NSURLIsExcludedFromBackupKey`), as are `files/` and `upload-staging/`
> beside it; the replica is unreadable before the first
> unlock after boot and readable afterwards while locked, which background wakes require and which
> matches the `AfterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly` class of the realm keys those wakes use (A1, A4
> route-1 amendments). **Relay exposure unchanged (House Rule #1 preserved):** device-local only; no
> key material, sync protocol or relay data shape changes.

**T-C-04, appended:**

> *Amendment (iOS shared replica, [`ios-shared-store-sqlite.md`](../proposals/ios-shared-store-sqlite.md)):*
> until this change no iOS code set `NSURLIsExcludedFromBackupKey` on the route-1 replica, so the
> checklist item above was not met for it on iOS. The replica's `replica/` directory now carries the
> flag, asserted at every open, and so do `files/` (`IosFileDatabase`) and `upload-staging/` in the
> same container, which had the same gap (decision D3b, 2026-10-03).

**T-T-08, appended (residual, no protocol change):**

> *Amendment (iOS shared replica, [`ios-shared-store-sqlite.md`](../proposals/ios-shared-store-sqlite.md) §5.4):*
> on iOS the device's durable HLC watermark lives in the shared replica's database, bound to the
> `(ownerId, deviceId)` it was raised under, with identity-bound per-app copies in the shared
> Keychain group (the floor is their maximum): **kept across a wipe of that replica, and across deleting every app, under the same
> identity, and void under any other**, so neither a wipe nor a reinstall under the same identity makes the
> tip a publish computes go backwards. (Two apps' requests can still reach the relay out of order,
> which the relay's last-write slot records as a regression: pre-existing, transient and GC-safe, and
> closed by a separate relay change, §15.1 R4 of that doc.) Residual (1), **the initial App Group cutover:** the shared store's
> watermark is not seeded from the app-local ones (they record no identity), so the device's first
> tip from it can sit below its relay slot and peers show a temporary `DIVERGENCE` (the T-T-04 tell)
> for that device, once, until its first local write or the cutover's re-pull carries the tip past
> the old value; the tracker then clears itself. Accepted deliberately: the alternative could raise
> a slot with a value its identity never observed. Residual (2): until the wiped store has re-pulled past
> it, the tip over-states what that store has applied, so the relay may drop, after the retention
> window, bodies of blocks below a tombstone the store has not yet re-pulled. The tombstone itself is
> retained, so the store still converges. Same-identity wipes are rare (a below-floor schema wipe, a
> reset corrupt store). Making the bound strict is the tip doc's O2 (split the wire), which would
> owe its own amendment.

**T-C-09, heading and first sentence:** "(Android/Desktop)" becomes "(Android/Desktop/iOS)", and a
sentence is added: "On iOS the same single-table blob store is `replica/objects.db` in the App-Group
container (A5 SQLite amendment), under `CompleteUntilFirstUserAuthentication` and excluded from
backup."

## Appendix B. S0b-1 slices 1 to 4, S0b-2 slices 1 to 3, the worker's walk, the hold watchdog, the open under it, the `REPLACEMENT` run on the worker, the UIKit adapter and the switched binding as built: the store core, the wipe and the migrator, the confirmed corruption code, the counted migration failure, protection and quiesce, the resumable confirmation walk, the hold watchdog, the open and the checkpoint under it, the job run off the launch path, the platform seam, the binding behind its switch (2026-10-18)

The first slices of S0b-1 are in `core-common/src/iosSqliteMain/…/proxy/db/sqlite/`, **bound
nowhere**: no DI line, no app. Slice 1 is the store core; slice 2 adds the chunked wipe
(§5.1, D13) and the chunked migrator (§5.3, D11); slice 3 confirms a corruption code on a second
connection before the durable marker is written (B.4's decision); slice 4 turns a migration whose
step fails on one row into a wipe at the `N`th run (B.3 (41), (53) to (56)). **S0b-2 slice 1** adds
rule P as a predicate, the tokens and quiesce (B.5, which carries its own choices and mutation
table). This appendix records what they cover, what they
leave to later slices, and the mechanism choices the sections above do not make. The sections above stay the design; where this
appendix differs it says so.

### B.1 What exists

| File | Holds |
|---|---|
| `ReplicaLimits.kt` | every constant of §4.2.1 in one value (`Wmax`, `C`, `G`, `ROW_MAX`, `MAX_DB_PAGES`, the 50 ms slice, `B_ckpt`), `N` of B.3 (41), and the arithmetic derived from them (`H`, `δ`, `journal_size_limit`, `fits`). The defaults are §4.2.1's placeholders, which Q0's device batch found holding warm |
| `ReplicaSchema.kt` | §2.2's layout stated once: the `CREATE` statements, schema validation and the wipe's table list are all derived from it |
| `ReplicaVerdicts.kt` | §5.2.2's table as one function, and the typed errors |
| `ReplicaClassification.kt` | the judgement of a store's versions against a build, a pure function used by both halves of the open |
| `ReplicaFiles.kt` | the store's own file-system calls behind one interface: the sidecar rule, the marker check, the `-wal` size probe |
| `ReplicaHandles.kt` | the handle registry of §2.8 and the gate: the admission count, labelled admissions, and since S0b-2 slice 1 the quiesce a reopen abandons and the waiting it hands to its protection (B.5) |
| `ReplicaProtection.kt` | S0b-2 slice 1: rule P as a predicate (§4.4), the tokens over a platform seam, the latch, the implicit token, the waiting, the shutdown (B.5) |

### B.3 Decisions made in implementation, for review

Each is the smallest thing found that keeps the invariants; none is a product decision.

1. **The marker check is an `fstat` of the directory, not a lookup by path.** Q0's device batch
   measured a `stat` by path at 16 to 24 µs and an `fstat` at 0.2 µs. A marker that does not exist
   has no descriptor, so the store keeps `replica/` open and `fstat`s that: writing the marker
   renames a file into the directory, which moves the directory's modification time. An unchanged
   time means an unchanged answer; the lookup by path runs only when the time moved. Two guards: a
   time is trusted only once it is 2 s in the past (a marker created in the same timestamp tick
   as the last change seen would otherwise be missed), and a descriptor that cannot be read falls
   back to the lookup by path. Once seen, the marker is latched for the process. **Cost per
   access: one `fstat`.** ⚠ Tested on the simulator (APFS on the Mac) only; that the phone's
   directory time moves on a rename is *GK*.
2. **The `-wal` size is an `fstat` on a read-only descriptor the store opens itself.** This is an
   exception to S1's wording ("nothing but a SQLite connection opens … `-wal`"). It is safe for
   the `-wal` alone: closing a descriptor drops the process's POSIX locks on that file, and SQLite
   takes none on the `-wal` (its WAL locks are byte ranges of `-shm`). Nothing is read or written
   through it; it is closed with the connection, and reopened if the file was unlinked behind it.
3. **Past `Wmax − δ` every outermost access gets `WalResetPending`, a read included.**
   `DatabaseLock.withLock` does not say whether its block writes, and every access is a
   `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` (§2.5), so "no transaction begins" is taken literally. The alternative, letting
   the block run and refusing its first write, would turn a retryable refusal into rule (a)'s fence.
   ⚠ A read that throws is new for callers; S0b-3's hosts must expect it.
4. **Protected data unavailable is judged before the result code** in §5.2.2's table, in every
   column, so no `CORRUPT` marker is ever written on evidence gathered while the phone is locked.
5. **A fenced handle is released at once**, at the exit of the access that fenced it, instead of
   waiting for the host's step 2b (§6): the rollback is issued where the failure is met and the
   connection closed at the outermost exit. The host's 2b then finds nothing to do.
6. **A marker that cannot be written is not reported as `CORRUPT`.** In an access the handle is
   fenced `COMMIT_FAILED` (in memory) instead; at open it is `StoreUnavailable`. The next process
   to meet the damage tries again.
7. **What a fenced handle answers to the three reads where "absent" is ambiguous:** `isEmpty()` is
   `false` (true would tell the sync cursor's self-heal the data was reset), `rowsOfTypes` and
   `scanRowsOfType` are `null` ("cannot enumerate", never an empty result), and the internal
   keyset pager throws, since its callers are jobs that must stop.
8. ⚠⚠ **`PRAGMA auto_vacuum` is never issued; the vendored SQLite is built with
   `SQLITE_DEFAULT_AUTOVACUUM=2`** (changed in review of slice 1; ⭐ **accepted by the maintainer,
   2026-10-07**, and §2.1.2, §2.3, §2.3.1 and §5.2 step 2a now say the same; they used to set it
   by pragma at creation). The pragma has to precede the
   first table, so it can only run before the write lock is held, on a file the open judged
   fresh a moment earlier; and on a store that exists it is a write transaction (Q0 results
   §11 (5)). No SQLite lock spans "is it fresh" and that pragma: `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` on an empty
   file writes page 1 itself, after which the pragma is refused. So an opener that lost a create
   race appended a frame to its sibling's store, and to a **newer** build's store before
   answering `SKEW` (S12, S19). The first version of this slice narrowed the window with a schema
   count just before the pragma; it did not close it. With the default compiled in, whichever
   connection first writes page 1 makes an incremental-vacuum database, the pragma is gone, and
   the freshness check and the create are both under `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`. The open reads
   `PRAGMA auto_vacuum` back as 2 beside `journal_mode`, and refuses the store otherwise.
   ⚠ This adds one option to D12's list (`scripts/build-sqlite-apple.sh`), and Q0's measurements
   were taken on the build without it, with the same on-disk result reached by pragma.
   ⚠ Found on the way: the cinterop task did not take the built static library as an input, so
   a rebuilt library was not relinked (`core-common/build.gradle.kts`, fixed in the same change).
9. **The rewind write also runs when the checkpoint reports an empty log.** A transaction that
   spilled and rolled back leaves the file large with no frame in the log; only the next commit
   truncates it (*Read:* `sqlite3.c`, `truncateOnCommit`), and the rewind write is that commit.
   And the reset is verified by size on **every** way out of the checkpoint, so a sibling that
   restarted the log first is believed too.
10. **The opportunistic checkpoint runs after a commit that leaves the `-wal` past `Wmax/4`** (§4.2.1's
    first trigger); the timer and end-of-job triggers wait for S0b-2.
11. **The keyset pager reads each type through `objects_type` and merges the pages.** One statement
    over several types would sort every matching row on every page.
12. **`StoreFull` is asked per growing statement**, with `PRAGMA page_count` and `freelist_count`
    (two prepared pragmas), exactly as §4.2.1 words it.
13. **A store marked "updating" is reported with its job only.** Whether this build may resume it
    is read from the marker's targets (§5.2 step 2), whose encoding belongs to the wipe's and the
    migrator's slices. The full compatibility check, which a marker never widens, is done here.
    ⚠ **Superseded in slice 2:** the marker's half of the resumer rule is now part of the same
    judgement (`classify`: the frame's format, a wipe's end stamps, a migration's targets), so the
    read-only classification answers `SKEW` for a marker this build may not resume, in the
    background as in the foreground, with no read/write connection (review of slice 2: decided
    only in the job's first transaction, a background open said "needs the foreground" and a
    foreground one opened read/write on a newer build's store before saying `SKEW`). Every job
    transaction runs the same `classify` again under the write lock.
14. **The gate here is an admission count with `closeAndDrain`**, open unless closed, and a refused
    access throws `ReplicaGateClosed`. Parking, `protect()` and the main-thread rule are S0b-2 (⭐ built in its slice 1, B.5; with no protection attached the gate still behaves as written here).
15. **The open's `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` and an access's share one slice loop** (§4.2), which leaves the
    gate and the in-process lock between slices.
16. **In the frozen marker, absent is never read as empty** (added in review of slice 1). §5.2
    step 2 says a file without `schema_service_versions` "is judged by the rest of the marker".
    Here that holds for a **newer** store only (`SKEW` on its layout or core version, nothing
    written). At or below this build's layout, a table that is missing, is not exactly the shape
    this build creates (B.3 (19)), or holds a row that is not `(text, integer)` is **damage**: `CORRUPT`, with the marker. Read as
    "no stamps" it made every declared service look unstamped and reported a damaged store as
    needing a migration; a stamp that is not an integer would have read as version 0 and asked
    for a wipe. A table that is present and well-formed with no row for a declared service is
    the unstamped service of §7: behind, not damaged. The two optional `meta` rows (`wipe`,
    `migration`) are judged by the row's existence, whatever it holds. ⚠ This closes the marker's
    own tables only: other damage on a store that is behind or marked (a dropped `objects`, say)
    is found by the validation of §5.2 step 3, which the job's slice runs before it starts
    anything (B.2).
17. **The registry's latch remembers what a failed close was for** (added in review of slice 1). A
    close that belonged to a release leaves the handle pending release, refused a connection,
    and the retry finishes the release (marked released, removed) before the process is usable
    again; a close for quiesce is retried as a close and the handle kept. Several handles can be
    stuck at once, and quiesce attempts every handle before it reports the first failure, so one
    failed close does not leave the others open across a suspension. **One function is the only
    way a close completes** (`connectionIsClosed`): it takes the handle off the latch and finishes
    a release that was owed, whoever asked for the close (a release, quiesce, the retry, a second
    release), so no path can close a handle and forget what the close was for.
18. **Each writer of `replica/CORRUPT` has its own temporary file** (added in review of slice 1):
    `CORRUPT.tmp.<pid>.<random>`, created `O_EXCL`, because two processes can detect the same
    damage at once and a shared name let one truncate or rename the other's. A writer whose own
    steps fail has still succeeded if the marker is there when it looks: it syncs the directory
    itself and reports `CORRUPT`, never a retry or `COMMIT_FAILED`, since corruption was
    detected. **A stray temporary file is ignored, not cleaned up:** the marker is looked up by
    its exact name only, nothing lists the directory, and nothing removes another writer's file
    (it may belong to a live writer). A writer removes its own on failure. The marker is the
    only file this slice writes by the temporary-then-rename rule.
    **"Already there" is not "already durable":** a marker found in place may be a rename no
    directory sync has followed yet. So a writer that finds one syncs the directory itself
    before it reports the store fenced (a failed sync is a failure, as after its own rename).
    ⚠⚠ **The invariant, one rule for every path: a marker is remembered, and reported as a
    durable fence, only after a successful directory sync by THIS process.** What a caller sees:

    | The marker is | At open | In an access or a checkpoint | Remembered |
    |---|---|---|---|
    | absent | goes on | goes on | the directory's time, by the rule of (1) |
    | there, and this process synced the directory | `Corrupt` | fenced `CORRUPT` | yes: never looked for again |
    | there, and the sync failed | **`StoreUnavailable`** (a retry; nothing opened read/write) | fenced **`COMMIT_FAILED`**, in memory | **no**: the next check looks again and syncs again |

    The third row refuses just as the second does (the file exists, and refusing is the safe
    direction); it differs only in what is claimed, and it is the same answer as a marker this
    process could not **write** (B.3 (6)), because it is the same shortfall. Checked against the
    invariant: `write` on both its ways out (its own rename, and a marker already there); the
    three finder paths (step 0 and the two later looks of the open, the check at the start of
    every access, the two checks of a checkpoint), which all go through one function; and the
    create path, which remembers nothing and syncs before its commit. The same for the store
    itself: the process that creates the store inside an `objects.db` that was already there
    (a sibling's empty file) syncs the directory in its creating transaction's path, before
    the commit. ⚠ Not done: syncing `replica/`'s **parent** when `replica/` is created or found;
    the design's sidecar rule names `replica/` only.
19. **The schema is compared as SQLite describes it, not as `sqlite_schema.sql` spells it** (added
    in review of slice 1). The expected description is read back, through the introspection
    pragmas, from an in-memory database made with the same `CREATE` statements a fresh store
    gets, so it is never written down twice. The pragmas were chosen over the `sql` text because
    that text keeps whitespace, quoting and keyword case, and a normaliser that is slightly
    wrong would call a healthy store `CORRUPT`, which is durable. Compared, for every object:
    a table's rowid or `WITHOUT ROWID`, `STRICT`, foreign keys, and per column position, name,
    declared type, `NOT NULL`, default, primary-key position and hidden or generated kind; an
    index's table, `UNIQUE`, origin, partial flag, and per column the column, direction and
    collation; the automatic indexes of constraints. **Any object beyond the layout's is
    damage**, an extra index, trigger or view on a store table included. The read-only
    classification applies the same description to `meta` and `schema_service_versions` before
    it believes a row of them. ⚠ Not visible to the pragmas, so not checked: a `CHECK`
    constraint, the collation of a column no index covers, a conflict clause, and the text of a
    partial index's `WHERE` or of an expression (that an index is partial or has an expression
    is seen).
20. **Absent, unreadable and ill-typed are three different answers, and none of them is a benign
    value** (added in review of slice 1; the rule behind (16) and (19) as well).
    - **A probe that fails throws; it never answers.** "Is the marker there", "how large is the
      `-wal`", "is there a file here" each have one failure that is an answer: nothing at the
      path (`ENOENT`, `ENOTDIR`). Any other (`EACCES`, `EMFILE`, `EIO`, a bad descriptor) is a
      `ReplicaFileException`. At the start of an access that is a retry
      (`StoreUnavailable`, or `ProtectedDataUnavailable` while the phone is locked), with the
      transaction rolled back and the handle not fenced; before a write statement inside a
      transaction the write is refused by rule (a); after a commit it is logged and no
      checkpoint is decided on it; after a checkpoint the reset is reported as **not** verified.
    - **`meta` is read by storage class.** `meta.v` keeps whatever is stored and SQLite reads a
      text or a blob as the integer 0, so every known row is checked at classification and in
      validation: `epoch` an integer; `seq` and `wal_rewind` an integer, not negative; `layout`
      an integer from 1 within 32 bits; `replaced_by` text; `wipe` and `migration` a blob with at
      least its format byte. A service stamp is an integer from 0 within 32 bits. Otherwise
      `CORRUPT`. `epoch` and `seq` are then read strictly, never coerced.
      ⚠ Two rows are deliberately **not** judged: `hlc_watermark`, whose malformed frame is
      decoded as "none" and overwritten (F6g, §11), and a key this build does not know, which a
      later slice of the same layout may add. ⚠ The two job markers are checked for being frames
      at all, not parsed: their encoding is their own slices'.
    - **`meta.wipe` and `meta.migration` together are damage**, not a priority order: the wipe's
      first chunk deletes the migration marker in the transaction that writes its own (§5.1).
      On a newer store this is still `SKEW` first, with nothing written.
    - **`user_version` is a version:** a negative one is damage, not "below the floor", which
      would have asked for a wipe.
    - **No default stands in for an answer nobody gave:** a `ReplicaBuild` must state a readable
      floor for every declared service (a missing one read as 0 would mean "migratable from any
      version"), the verdict table must be told whether protected data is available, and an
      access that reaches its end with no connection to commit on is fenced `COMMIT_FAILED`
      instead of returning as if it had committed.
21. **A `ROLLBACK` that fails is an access failure, not something to log and go on from** (added
    in review of slice 1). Where the access means to continue after it (before the ceiling
    checkpoint, before a retryable refusal at the start of an access, after a transaction found
    left open), a failed rollback fences the handle `COMMIT_FAILED`, which releases it and closes
    the connection (or latches the process, the registry's rule), and the access throws: never a
    checkpoint attempted over a connection that may still hold the write lock, and never a
    retryable answer on one. The quiet form remains only inside a fence, where the release that
    follows at once rolls back again as it closes. The same for the `ROLLBACK` of an access whose
    gate closed while it waited: on failure the connection is closed.
22. **The classification gathers every fact before it answers** (added in review of slice 1). The
    layout, the core version and every service stamp are each compared with this build and with
    its floor, and the markers read, with no early return; the verdict is then derived in one
    place, in this precedence: anything above this build is `SKEW`; damaged bookkeeping is
    `CORRUPT`; a job marker is "updating"; **anything** below its floor is a wipe; anything
    behind is a migration; otherwise compatible. The first form answered "behind, a migration"
    at the first thing it found behind, so a store with an older layout **and** a stamp below
    its floor was reported as migratable. A test walks all 160 combinations of layout, core,
    one service and the markers against an expectation written from this list.
23. **The opener owns what it acquires until it hands a live store back** (added in review of
    slice 1). That is the directory descriptor the marker check keeps open (B.3 (1)) and every
    handle the open registered, with its connection. `Ready` is the one hand-over, to the store,
    which gives them back when its handle is released (a close, a fence). Every other way out,
    each verdict and each throw, releases all of it in **one `finally`** that each entry point
    (`open`, and the two halves a test calls separately) runs under; no branch closes the
    marker for itself. The first form closed it branch by branch and missed step 0's throws and
    its orphaned-sidecar return: one descriptor per failed open, until `EMFILE`. A handle is
    still released earlier where the open goes on after it (the classification's connection
    before the read/write one), which only takes it off the list that `finally` empties.
    The test repeats every kind of open that does not end in a store and counts the process's
    descriptors before and after, by asking the kernel about each number, so SQLite's are seen
    too. ⚠ The `-wal` descriptor of B.3 (2) is never the opener's: the store opens it at its
    first access.
24. **`fsync` stands in for `F_FULLFSYNC` only where it was refused as not supported** (`ENOTSUP`,
    `ENOTTY`; added in review of slice 1). Any other failure of the flush is a failed sync, so by
    B.3 (18) the marker is not remembered and not reported durable. The first form fell back
    after every failure, so an `EIO` from the flush followed by an `fsync` that succeeded was
    reported as a durable fence. Apple's `fcntl(2)` names no `errno` for this: it says only
    that `F_FULLFSYNC` "is currently implemented on HFS, MS-DOS (FAT), Universal Disk Format
    (UDF) and APFS file systems". `ENOTSUP` is measured (a directory on devfs, macOS 26.6,
    pinned by a test); `ENOTTY` is by reading, not measured (the call reaches the file system
    as an ioctl). **The fallback is not expected to run in production:** `replica/` is on APFS
    in the group container, where the call is accepted on a directory descriptor on the phone
    and on the Mac (Q0 (q)). It is logged when it runs. ⚠ `EINTR` is not retried: it is a
    failed sync, which is the safe direction.

**Slice 2 (the wipe and the migrator), 2026-10-07.** Where one of these differs from a section
above it says which.

25. **The chunked migrator is a driver of its own in `iosSqliteMain`, not a `Chunked` sink inside
    `StoreSchemaMigrator`** (**this differs from §5.3's table**, which adds `pagesOfTypes`, a
    `checkpoint` parameter and a `StepSink` to shared code). The two migrators share exactly one
    thing, what a step makes of one row, and that is already a function of its own
    (`StoreRowMigrationCodec.migrateRow`). Everything else in the chunked mode (the marker, the
    phases, the cursor, the bookkeeping tables, the budget) has no JVM counterpart, so a sink
    would have been an interface with one implementation on each side and nothing in common. The
    driver takes its chains as `ReplicaMigrationSteps` (a step: the types it reads, and
    `migrate(row)`). **`:core-common` commonMain is untouched**, so "the JVM and Android are
    unchanged" (§5.3) holds by construction and not by a test.
    ⚠ `SchemaMigration.droppedProperties` was added after §5.3 was written and §5.3 does not
    mention it: the JVM migrator strips those slots from **every** stored row of the type, on top
    of the composite rewrite. The adapter must put those types in the step's `typeIds` and strip
    in its `migrate`; it is the binding slice's (B.2), and a step whose only content is a dropped
    property would otherwise read no row on iOS.
26. **`meta.epoch` is read at every outermost access, under the write lock, with no `data_version`
    fast path** (§3.1 step 2, taken early from the cache's slice). A handle whose epoch is not
    its open's is fenced `REPLACED`. Without it "nothing serves a half-wiped store" was true of
    new opens only: a sibling that was already open went on reading the rows a wipe had not
    reached yet. Cost: one indexed read per access (about 4 µs, §3.1), until the fast path lands.
27. **A damage verdict reached under the write lock writes `replica/CORRUPT` before the lock is
    given up**, at open and in a job chunk alike (looked at in this slice because slice 1 left it
    unstated). That is §5.2.1's "inside its transaction if it holds the write lock" and it is
    what §3.1 step 0 rests on: a sibling that began after the lock was released and before the
    marker existed would pass its own marker check and commit to a store already judged damaged.
    The price is two `F_FULLFSYNC`s with the write lock held, which §4.2.1's watchdog table
    exempts. Slice 1 did this in its `catch` blocks and **not** on the schema-validation path,
    which rolled back first; that path now writes first too, and a test asks a sibling for the
    write lock while the marker is being renamed into place.
28. **The store's `-wal` descriptor is kept only while its handle's connection is open** (B.3 (2)
    said "closed with the connection", which a measurement after the close broke: the descriptor
    was reopened and then had nothing left to close it, across a suspension after a quiesce and
    for good after a release). A measurement with no connection now opens, measures and closes.
29. **One checkpoint implementation, and it never throws** (`ReplicaCheckpointer`, taken out of
    the store so a job chunk runs the same one). Its step-0 look for the marker was outside its
    `try`, so a lookup that failed escaped as a different refusal; it is "skipped" now, and the
    ceiling answers `WalResetPending` for every way a reset can fail to be verified.
30. **The open of a marked or behind store hands back no store at all:** `Updating(job,
    replacement)`, where §5.2 step 3 says "returns the runtime's handle fenced `UPDATING` and
    registers a `REPLACEMENT` handle". A handle that can never serve is only a way to use it by
    mistake, and no `RUNTIME` handle is registered, so the rebuild has nothing to wait for. The
    `REPLACEMENT` handle is registered per **run** (§2.8), not by the open. `NeedsReplacement`
    is gone: a foreground open of a store that is behind **starts** the job, in one transaction
    with the validation of the recorded layout's schema (`ReplicaReplacement.admit`).
31. **The marker frames** (`ReplicaJobMarkers.kt`). The first byte is the format. A frame of
    another format is a newer build's: `SKEW`, nothing written. A frame of this format that does
    not parse is damage (B.4 path 8), **and so is one no writer produces, though every field
    parses** (an unstamped step with a phase or a cursor, a cleanup with a cursor, text that is
    not UTF-8, a byte left over): read leniently, each of those turns damage into `SKEW` or,
    worse, into a step that stamps a service over rows nobody migrated. `meta.wipe`: reason, app, start time, the stamps to write
    at the end. `meta.migration`: app, start time, the targets, the current step (service,
    `from`), the phase, the cursor with an explicit "none". ⚠ **Any change to either frame is a
    new format byte**, or an older build would read the new frame as damage and mark the store.
    (Slice 4's count is format 2 of `meta.migration`, used only while a count is stored: (54).)
32. **`:core` is in the marker as the service `tenshu/core`** (`CORE_SERVICE_ID`), stamped in
    `user_version` where every other service is a row of `schema_service_versions`; §5.3's marker
    names services only. **A declared service with no stamp is a step of the chain too**
    (`from` = none): it is stamped at its target with no row read, the JVM migrator's rule ("no
    earlier build could have written its rows"), inside the fence and at a step finish like any
    other stamp.
33. **A store whose `meta.layout` is behind is refused, retryably** (`StoreUnavailable`, nothing
    written), **before its schema is validated and whatever else is true of it**: marked or not,
    for an open, a resumer and a wipe alike (review of slice 2: validated first, against this
    layout's schema, a healthy older store would have been marked `CORRUPT` for good). **It is a
    verdict of the classification itself** (`OlderLayout`, after `SKEW` and before damage), so
    the read-only half answers it and no read/write connection is opened on a store this build
    will refuse; every job transaction meets the same verdict again under the lock. §2.2 says the layout "is judged like a service version", but §5.3's steps migrate
    rows, and what a layout step does (DDL, behind which fence) is not designed. No such store
    can exist while there is one layout.
34. **The verification is a phase of its own, `VERIFY`, and it is the row loop read a second
    time** from before the first row: every row of the step's types is looked up in
    `migration_done`, and one that is not there is migrated then and there. §5.3 counts first
    and re-runs the row phase "over exactly those"; one pass that does both has no window
    between the count and the re-run, and needs a cursor only for its own paging. A row that is
    recorded is never migrated again, in either pass.
35. ⚠⚠ **`δ` guarantees one statement, and a migration object is up to five** (**a hole in
    §4.2.1**: "rule 1 lets a transaction begin only at or below `Wmax − δ`, so every row
    operation `ROW_MAX` allows fits in one transaction"). An object's statements are admitted
    together (its rewrite, `meta.seq`, `migration_done`, `migration_dropped`, the cursor), so a
    chunk can begin under the ceiling and find that its **first** object does not fit. It then
    rolls back, runs the ceiling checkpoint and tries again, three times, before the run stops
    with `WalResetPending`. That converges only if a reset log leaves the room:
    `Wmax/4 + C + U ≤ Wmax`, with `U = max(H + 3G, h(0, ROW_MAX) + 4G)`: a `ROW_MAX` rewrite is
    `H` with three single-row statements beside it, a dropped row `h(0, ROW_MAX)` with four, and
    which is larger depends on `G` against the overflow chain (equal at the placeholders, the
    dropped row larger in the tests' small limits; review of slice 2 caught the first form of
    this, which counted the rewrite only). At the placeholders that is 750 + 256 + 1,536 =
    2,542 of 3,000: true.
    **`ReplicaLimits` refuses to be constructed otherwise**, naming the terms, so whoever moves
    `Wmax`, `C`, `G` or `ROW_MAX` meets it at startup and in every test. The statements of a start, a step finish and a finish are admitted one
    by one instead (they are all-or-nothing by rolling back, in transactions that did nothing
    else).
36. **`meta.seq` moves in every chunk that writes `objects`** (S4, taken literally), where §5.1's
    statements show it only in the first chunk. The epoch moves at a start and a finish only.
37. **What a wipe call does on a store that is not in step.** *Behind this build, or
    mid-migration:* the marker carries this build's versions for the last chunk to stamp. The
    store is empty by then, and left at its old stamps it would be migrated, or wiped a second
    time, by the next open. Only a build that could have resumed the migration may wipe over
    it. *Already marked `meta.wipe`:* joined, the marker and its end stamps kept, no second
    start. *No `objects.db`, or one never made into a store:* nothing to wipe, and nothing is
    created. *Newer, or marked corrupt:* `WipeRefused`, after a read-only classification and
    with no read/write connection opened (S19). **Its step 0 is the open's own**, asked not to
    create a file (found in review of slice 2: a copy of those lookups called a sidecar without
    its `objects.db` "nothing to wipe", which the next open fences as corruption).
38. **A wipe's first chunk on a live handle that fails on a statement fences the handle
    `COMMIT_FAILED`**, by rule (a), where §4.2.1's watchdog table says the handle is left
    unfenced. Nothing was written and no marker exists either way, and one rule for every
    statement of every access is worth more than the exception. A first chunk that never began
    (the gate, `WalResetPending`) leaves the handle serving.
39. **The hold ceiling, as far as it needs no timer:** a job's transaction measures its hold
    from the moment `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` returns (the marker lookup and the `-wal` probe that
    follow run under the lock, so a slow one counts; found in review of slice 2), and a statement
    or a `COMMIT` reached after `HOLD_MAX` is refused (`HoldCeilingExceeded`): rolled back, the
    run stops. ⚠ The runtime handle's ordinary accesses measure no hold at all yet: theirs is
    S0b-2's watchdog, which must start its clock at the same point. That is the watchdog's
    between-statements half; interrupting a statement while it runs needs S0b-2's timer queue.
    The chunk's stops (the budget, `chunkMaxRows`, `chunkTimeStopMs`) and `HOLD_MAX` are in
    `ReplicaLimits`.
40. **A chain cut out from under its marker becomes a wipe inside the chunk that finds it**
    (§5.3's marker rule): that chunk is a wipe's first, so the epoch moves there. It needs no
    foreground of its own, since a migration only runs in one.
41. ⭐ **A migration step that fails on one and the same row becomes a wipe in the `N`th run that
    meets it** (decided by the maintainer, 2026-10-07 and 2026-10-10; **built in slice 4**, whose
    mechanism is (53) to (56)). Not "skip the row", not "stay fenced": the device re-syncs from
    the relay, the outcome a chain with no registered step already has ((40)). Before slice 4 the
    run stopped and changed nothing, every time, and the store stayed "Updating storage…" for
    every app until a fixed build arrived (the JVM fails its open the same way, but there the old

    - **The count is durable, in `meta.migration`**, keyed to the failing position (the marker's

      step's service**. A build that declares another version starts at one. **The frame keeps
      one count, the last counter's.**

    - **`N` = 3, `ReplicaLimits.migrationRowAttempts`, and at most one count per run of the

      different versions and take turns reset each other and never reach `N`.** And a wipe can
      follow from one row this build cannot read, where the JVM would keep failing its open.
42. **Every touch of the database a job makes is inside a gate admission** (found in review of
    slice 2). A chunk that rolls back to reset the log gives its admission back, and the ceiling
    checkpoint that follows ran outside any: `closeAndDrain` could answer "drained" with a
    `RESTART` checkpoint and its rewind write still to come, under a quiesce that is closing
    every connection. The checkpoint now takes an admission of its own and is not started once
    the gate has closed. `ReplicaCheckpointer` enters no gate itself: each caller is inside one
    (the runtime handle's access at the ceiling and after a commit; a job's transaction after a
    commit; a job's own admission for the reset). **The same for what follows a failure:** an
    access or an open that fails rolls back and closes its connection before it leaves the gate,
    never after. **And `replica/CORRUPT` is written inside an admission or not now**
    (`admittedForMarker`): §4.2.1 has quiesce wait for a marker write in progress, which it can
    only do for one that is counted; a damage verdict reached with no admission (step 0's

    ⚠ Not closed: `ReplicaCorruptMarker.state()` syncs the directory when it first finds a
    sibling's marker, and the open's step 0 asks it outside any admission.
    **A close is counted too, at the one place every close goes through**
