### B.8 The worker's slice, carrying the resumable walk (Q5) (2026-10-16)

**What it is.** Q5's decision in code, bound nowhere. The operation that meets a corruption code
(B.4 paths 5, 6, 7 and 9) no longer reads the store a second time. It is fenced as before, gives up
its connection, looks for a sibling's marker, and **hands the code off** to this app's
**confirmation walk**. The **worker** runs the walk off the access, in runs of at most `CONFIRM_MAX`.
Each run holds a job token of its own (`acquireForJob`) and has its own admission check, and the walk
carries its position across runs, wakes and process deaths. It ends the way the inline reading did:
**damage**, and `replica/CORRUPT` written (only while protected data is available), or **every unit
read without a finding**, and the walk is over. Until it ends, **this app's opens are refused** with
`StoreBeingChecked`, which is the `COMMIT_FAILED` fence held across runs and wakes, a cost Q5
accepts. The B.3 (47) ship blocker is therefore **resolved in code**: a cold store of any size is
read whole in the end. What it still owes is the device's figures (B.8.6).

**What "the worker's slice" also names, and what was split off.** B.2 and B.5.3 give the worker's
slice more than the walk. This slice builds the walk and the minimal worker the walk needs: a token
per run, taken off the main thread with no registry lock held ((86), asserted by `acquireForJob`).
**Split off, and not built here:**

| Not built | Why not here | Where |
|---|---|---|
| The `REPLACEMENT` run on the worker: running `ReplicaReplacement.run` off the launch path after `Updating`, a token per run, installing the runtime at the finish | installing the runtime needs S0b-3's host. `ReplicaWorker` is generic enough to take it (a job, a token per run, runs while advancing) | ⭐ *built in B.11, but for installing the runtime: the host's reopen after `Finished` (S0b-3)* |
| `run` refusing a migration chunk outside the foreground (B.2) | belongs to the `REPLACEMENT` run above | ⭐ *built in B.11 (146)* |
| What a host does with a run that counted (`MigrationRowFailed`: "not again before the next foreground") | same | ⭐ *built in B.11 (147), in the worker* |
| A wipe call holding one token for the whole call | it changes `wipeAllObjects`'s callers, who are bound only by the binding slice | the binding slice |
| The worker's triggers at a foreground and a wake (`ReplicaWorker.kick()`), and its serial queue | UIKit; the adapter is not built (B.5.3) | S0b-2, with the adapter |
| The hold watchdog; the 30 s and end-of-job checkpoint triggers | S0b-2's own items, not the worker's (§13) | S0b-2, later slices |
| "Checking storage…" on screen | S0b-3's surface (B.8.5) | S0b-3 |

#### B.8.1 What exists

| Piece | What it does | Where |
|---|---|---|
| The hand-off | ⚠ *Since the fix round, never for a checkpoint's code (113).* `ReplicaCorruptionConfirm.run`: close the failing connection, look for a sibling's marker (gate open), then `walk.request(error)`. It is in memory only, so it is made also with the gate closed. Returns `Unconfirmed(handedOff = true)`, which each path already treats as its retry (B.3 (49)). The 20 ms pause, the second reading and `quick_check` left this class. (52)'s rule (the second checkpoint code in a row confirms with no reading) is unchanged | `ReplicaCorruptionConfirm.kt` |
| The walk | `ReplicaConfirmationWalk`, one per registry and app (`ReplicaHandles.confirmationWalk`). A run is one gate admission and `CONFIRM_WALK`'s time check, then the marker lookup, the pause, a refusal while this process holds a transaction, and up to `CONFIRM_MAX` of reading on a `CLASSIFY` connection (`readOnly`, the classification read first, `cell_size_check` on). It ends in the marker, the end of the walk, or the position made durable | `ReplicaConfirmationWalk.kt` |
| The units | `WHOLE` (`quick_check(1)` over the file). Only if that is bounded: `TABLE` (`quick_check(<t>)`) for every table but `objects`, `ROWS` (every row of `objects` by `hash` keyset, every column), `INDEX` (every entry of `objects_type` by `(type, hash)` keyset), and `SCHEMA` (`quick_check(sqlite_schema)`, the schema tree and the free list) last. All derived from `ReplicaSchema` | `ReplicaWalkUnit` |
| The position | `replica/confirm-walk.<app>`, written by the sidecar rule (temporary file, `F_FULLFSYNC`, `rename`, directory sync), FNV-1a checksummed, bound to the format, the app, the layout, the unit list and `meta.epoch` | `ReplicaWalkPosition` |
| The fence | `ReplicaOpener.open`, after step 0, answers `StoreBeingChecked` (a `StoreCorruptionUnconfirmed`) while this app's walk is owed in memory or on disk, and schedules it again. The open's own hand-off (path 5) answers the same | `SharedReplicaStoreOpen.kt`, `ReplicaVerdicts.kt` |
| The admission | `ReplicaOperation.CONFIRM_WALK` = `CONFIRM_MAX` + the 20 ms pause + `R` + `2·S_full` + the 2 s margin, which is 4.22 s at the placeholders. Short of it, the run is `Deferred` with nothing opened | `ReplicaAdmissionBudget.kt` |
| The worker | `ReplicaWorker`: `attach` makes every hand-off schedule its walk. Each run is under one `acquireForJob` token released when the run returns, and runs follow each other while each advances. A walk already dispatched is marked to run again rather than dispatched twice. A refused token (the main thread, a lock holder) is logged and answered `NotMade`, never thrown on a dispatch queue | `ReplicaConfirmationWalk.kt` |
| A small-file read | `ReplicaFiles.readAll(path, maxBytes)`: null only when absent, a throw for anything larger or unreadable | `ReplicaFiles.kt` |

#### B.8.2 One run, in order

1. **The gate**: `enter`, refused → `Deferred`. Closing → `Deferred`. Then `CONFIRM_WALK`'s time
   check → `Deferred`, before any file work.
2. **Where to start**: the position in memory, else the one on disk (read once per process), else a
   fresh one if a code was handed off here. Nothing owed → `NothingPending`.
3. **A sibling's marker** → the verdict (`Confirmed`), and the walk is over.
4. **The pause** (20 ms). Then the gate is asked again, and a transaction of this process's own
   defers the run.
5. **The reading**, stopped by the progress handler at `CONFIRM_MAX`, when the gate closes, or at an
   expiry (`stop()`). It begins with the classification read and `meta.epoch`. A position from
   another epoch starts over at `WHOLE`. Then the units, from the position on.
6. **The conclusion.** Damage, with protected data available → the marker, and the walk is over;
   without it → `NotMade`. Read to the end → the marker looked for once more, then `Clean`: the
   position is removed and the walk owes nothing. Bounded → the position saved (not once the gate is
   closing). Stopped by the gate → `Deferred`, nothing saved.

#### B.8.3 Decisions made in implementation, for review

Numbered on from B.7.

101. **The hand-off is in memory; the walk is durable from its first reading.** A process killed
     between the code and the walk's first run leaves nothing, and the next open judges the store,
     exactly as before Q5 (B.3 (50), "a kill between the fence and the second reading"). Writing a
     file at the hand-off would mean file work under the failing access's lock and admission, and a
     file written with the gate closed. The cost is that a code met just before a kill is forgotten
     until the damage is met again.
102. **Where the position lives, and why a bad one can only cost runs.** In
     `replica/confirm-walk.<app>`, **not in the database**: the store is suspect, and the walk reads
     it on a read-only connection (step 1 of (45): nothing more is written through it). Crash safety
     rests on four rules, each tested:
     - (a) It is written by the sidecar rule, so a crash leaves the old file or the new one.
     - (b) A file that does not decode (a torn write, a flipped bit, another format, app, layout or
       unit list) is **no position**: the walk starts at `WHOLE`. It is still "owed", so the fence
       holds.
     - (c) A key is recorded only once SQLite has **returned** its row or entry, never the key a
       stopped statement was on. And a run stopped before it had read `meta.epoch` saves nothing.
     - (d) A saved position is never ahead of what was read, so a stale one (a later save lost to
       power loss) is behind and costs re-reading.

     So unread pages can never count as read. The removal at the end is not synced: a lost removal
     brings back a position, and the walk reads its last units again and ends again.
103. **How a page-ranged check is done, against SQLite 3.53.4's own source** (the vendored
     `sqlite3.c`; each line below was read there, not assumed). `quick_check` is not resumable, but:
     - `PRAGMA quick_check(<table>)` checks that one table's B-trees (the table and its indexes),
       and the free list only when the table is `sqlite_schema` (`PragTyp_INTEGRITY_CHECK`, its
       comment "The freelist is only verified if the named table is sqlite_schema", and
       `sqlite3BtreeIntegrityCheck`'s `bCkFreelist`). Such a *partial* check skips the "every page
       is referenced" pass, the max-root-page check and the root pages' pointer-map check
       (`bPartial`).
     - A keyset `SELECT` of every column loads each value whole: `OP_Column` reads an overflowing
       value through `vdbeColumnFromOverflow` → `sqlite3BtreePayload`, so a row's overflow chain is
       read.
     - `PRAGMA cell_size_check = ON` (`SQLITE_CellSizeCk`) makes `btreeInitPage` run
       `btreeCellSizeCheck` on every page it loads.

     So the ranged walk reads every leaf and overflow page of `objects` and every page of its index
     through SQLite's own page checks, and quick-checks the small tables, the schema and the free
     list whole. ⚠ **What it does not check that `WHOLE` does:** a page referenced twice or never;
     key order and bounds across pages (`checkTreePage`'s `maxKey`); the index entry count against
     the table's; the pointer map of `objects`' pages; `quick_check`'s per-row record checks on
     `objects` beyond what reading every column checks. ⚠ *GK, unverified:* that an ordered scan
     visits every interior page of a tree (it follows from how a cursor descends and ascends, and it
     is not measured; `dbstat` would show it, and this build does not have it). The trade was taken
     because an access meets damage through the same page-loading paths the walk takes. Damage only
     a whole-file pass sees is not damage an access reports with a code. **`WHOLE` comes first**, so
     every store that fits in one run (every cached store, and about 47,000 pages cold) still gets
     exactly (46)'s check.
104. **The small tables are walked whole, one unit each.** They are small by construction:
     `meta`, `schema_service_versions`, `schedule_lease` (its key cap), and the migration's two key
     tables, which hold at most one integer per row (a 150,000-row store's `migration_done` is a few
     hundred pages). ⚠ A unit that cannot finish inside one run never advances. The worker stops at a
     run that did not advance, and the walk would never end. Not expected, and logged.
105. **Sibling commits and checkpoints between runs do not restart the walk; a new epoch does.**
     The walk is logical, by key, through SQLite's own reads, so a checkpoint changes nothing it can
     see. A row a sibling writes behind the walk's position was written by SQLite from pages it
     had loaded and checked. A row written ahead of it is read when the walk gets there. A row's key
     never moves. A wipe, a migration or a replacement moves `meta.epoch`, and the walk starts over.
     Restarting on every sibling commit (on `meta.seq`) would never end on a store with an active
     sibling. **Open question Q9.**
106. **The fence is this app's alone.** `StoreBeingChecked` refuses this app's opens while its walk
     is owed. A sibling is not held back, exactly as it was not by the inline reading (45): only the
     marker fences another process. One walk per app, with its own position file, so two apps never
     write one file. **Open question Q11.**
107. **A run holds the registry's lock while it reads**, as the inline reading did ((45), accepted
     2026-10-10), but now on the worker's thread, never on the thread that met the code. A run
     **does not read while this process holds a transaction** (`Deferred`), as before.
108. **The worker, minimal.** A token per run (B.2: "its token per run"). Runs follow each other
     while each advances; any other outcome ends the dispatch and is told to the host
     (`onOutcome`). It is scheduled by a hand-off, by an open refused for an owed walk, and by the
     host's `kick()` (not built). An expiry sets the walk's stop flag, which the progress handler
     reads. `acquireForJob`'s refusal is answered `NotMade` and logged, not thrown, since a throw on
     a dispatch queue ends the process.
109. ~~A checkpoint's first code hands off too.~~ ⚠ **Superseded by (113)** (fix round):
     a checkpoint's code never goes to the walk.
110. ⚠ **Found on the way: SQLite does not seek a row value on an index plus its rowid.**
     `WHERE (type, hash) > (?, ?)` on `objects_type` plans as `SEARCH … (type>?)`, a `SeekGE` on
     `type` alone with the rowid filtered (measured, and seen in `EXPLAIN`). Every run therefore
     re-read the entries of the type it had stopped in from the first one, and a store whose rows
     share a type never got past one run's worth. The test run spun for hours on it. The keyset is
     now two statements (`type = ? AND hash > ?`, then `type > ?`), and the plan test asserts
     `(type=? AND rowid>?)`.
111. **A whole-file check that is bounded moves the walk to the ranged units.** It is never tried
     twice on one store: a check that did not finish in one run will not finish in the next, cold.
     That an attempt warms the cache is true and still not relied on (B.3 (47)).

**Fix round of the independent review (2026-10-16).**

112. ⚠⚠ **The index keyset carries its `type` key as the raw bytes SQLite stored**, never a
     decoded string. `getText` decodes with replacement, so a damaged type such as `Fi\x80le`
     resumed as `Fi\uFFFDle`, which sorts after it. `type > ?` then skipped every remaining entry
     of the real type, and the walk could end `Clean` over entries it never read. That was a hole
     in the soundness of the verdict. The key is now read with `sqlite3_column_blob`, kept hex in
     the position file, and bound back as TEXT of exactly those bytes (`bindTextBytes`).
     Tested with a malformed type spanning run boundaries. A run is stopped deterministically
     inside that type, and the test asserts a saved position there with entries of the type after
     it.
     ⚠⚠ **Superseded by B.9 (122): the keyset is storage-class-aware and steps past an entry of
     any class; a NULL or a number in a row's `type` is damage, as `quick_check` says.** What
     follows is the second fix round's design, kept for the record.
     ⚠ **Revised in the second fix round: a `type` that is not TEXT ends the walk with no
     verdict**, as `Stalled` ("could not be checked"), and **not** as damage. `quick_check` does
     not flag a BLOB in a non-STRICT TEXT column, so calling it damage would make the verdict
     depend on the store's size: the same row would be `Clean` at `WHOLE` on a small store and
     marked for good on a large one. And (45) wants two readings that agree. **The keyset stops
     there and steps past nothing.** Ordering by storage class was not built: `type = ?` and
     `type > ?` compare across classes through the column's affinity, so a sound resume across
     classes would need statements per class. **No writer in this codebase can produce such a
     row:** `UPSERT_SQL` binds `type` with `bindText`, and the column is `TEXT NOT NULL`.
113. ⚠⚠ **A checkpoint's code never starts a walk** (the coordinator's choice; it replaces (109)).
     By (52), `quick_check` reads through the log and its index, which is what a checkpoint's code
     is about, so a walk could never confirm one. It would only fence this app's opens for many
     runs, and hold the registry's lock about a second a run under a live runtime. **(52) is the
     whole handling:** the first code is "skipped" (a sibling's marker is still the verdict), and
     the next code in a row, on another connection, is the confirmation.
     ⚠ **A known cost, for the codes that do reach the walk** (an access's, the open's, a job's):
     each run holds `registry.lock` for up to about 1 s, with gaps of about 20 ms between runs. A
     store with a live runtime of this process waits on it. Today the runtime that met the code is
     fenced, so that is its rebuild and any job. A run deferred because this process holds a
     transaction is rescheduled only by the next hand-off, an open, or `kick()`.
114. **"Owed" has one test, and a file that cannot be removed does not fence this process for
     good.** `isPending()` and the run's starting position read the same thing: memory, else the
     file on disk, re-read whenever memory knows no position. So a file another process of the
     same name wrote is seen. A position file this process ended on and could not remove is
     remembered by its bytes, and is neither owed nor walked again here. A later save replaces
     it, and a new process walks it once more. **The file is named by the hex of the app's name**
     (`confirm-walk.<hex>`), so no two names share one, where the sanitised `a/b` and `a_b` did.
115. **A walk that cannot advance is logged and, after `STALL_RUNS` runs in a row, `Stalled`.**
     `STALL_RUNS` = 3 is a placeholder. A run that ended where it began is logged. At
     `STALL_RUNS` the walk is **terminal in this process**: no further run, the fence kept, and
     the open answers `StoreBeingChecked(stalled = true)`, which the surface shows as "could not be
     checked". The next launch tries again from the saved position. Lifting the fence instead was
     not chosen: that is the pre-Q5 loop of code, fence and retry. **An open's refusal schedules
     the walk at most once per `OPEN_RESCHEDULE_MS`**, a 5 s placeholder. A schedule suppressed
     in the window is **owed, not dropped**: one is dispatched when the window ends (second fix
     round). A restart counts as
     progress only when the position named a known store that changed, so a store whose epoch or
     file cannot be read stalls instead of restarting forever.
116. **A request made while a run reads is not lost.** Each request moves a serial, and a run
     that ends the walk clears only the requests it started under. The worker's "run again" mark
     then runs the walk again. Both are needed and both are tested (M95, M96).
117. **An expiry before the run begins still stops it.** The stop flag is the run's own
     (`ReplicaWalkStop`), made before `acquireForJob` and passed to the run. Previously `run()`
     cleared a shared flag after the token was taken, so an expiry in between was lost.
118. **Nits, each in code** (⚠ the first bullet below is revised by (121)):
     - The position carries a fingerprint of the whole unit list.
     - `rowsSql`'s columns are derived from `ReplicaSchema`, keyed by its `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY`
       and checked like the index's shape.
     - An unknown epoch or file never matches, on either side.
     - The `Clean` branch looks for a sibling's marker only with the gate open.
     - The position is bound to the database file's `dev:ino` (by `stat` on the path, no
       descriptor), so an older copy restored under the same epoch starts the walk over.
     - ⚠ A stale position file can outlive a sibling's `CORRUPT` marker. That is harmless: the next
       run finds the marker first, answers `Confirmed`, and removes the file.

**Second fix round (targeted re-review of `ed6a80b`, 2026-10-16).**

119. **A stall lifts within the process, and an expiry is never a stall.** A run while stalled
     still reads the classification and `meta.epoch`, and nothing further, on the store it stalled
     on (`Stalled` again, cheaply). It lifts the stall when the epoch or the file's `dev:ino`
     changed, which is a sibling's wipe or replacement. A new hand-off (`request`) lifts it too:
     a new code is new evidence. A run ended by its token's expiry (`stop.asked`) does not count
     toward `STALL_RUNS`; the platform cut it short, not the store. An open of a stalled walk is
     rescheduled at the rate limit like any other, so a sibling's wipe is noticed without a
     relaunch.
120. **A position file that cannot be read is a position that does not decode.** If `readAll`
     throws (over its 16 KiB bound, or an I/O error), the walk is still owed and starts fresh,
     and the next save's `rename` replaces the file. Before this, every open threw
     `StoreUnavailable` and every run was `NotMade`. The end of a walk removes such a file too.
     If it can be neither read nor removed, this process remembers that and does not walk it
     again.
121. ⚠⚠ **An unreadable `meta.epoch` is damage, by the open's own rule** (it revises (118)'s
     "unknown never matches" for the epoch). Read as "unknown", it made every run restart at
     unit 0, stall after `STALL_RUNS`, and do so again at every launch. Meanwhile the open's own
     judgement (`metaInteger` → `ReplicaDamaged` → `Corrupt`) never ran, since `refusedWhileChecked`
     comes before `readAndJudge`. So the store was never marked, exported or replaced: B.3 (47)
     again, for one input. The walk now concludes damage there, which is the verdict the open
     would reach (the walk's run is the second reading of a code already met). The file identity
     can still be unknown (`stat` finds nothing at the path), and an unknown file still never
     matches. ⚠ **Gated on the layout since B.9 (123)**, and it marks on one read-only snapshot
     (B.9 (126)).

#### B.8.4 Open questions for the maintainer

⭐ **Q9 to Q13 DECIDED by the maintainer, 2026-10-16, as recommended**, with two statements made
plain:
- **Q9: "checked" means each key as of when the walk read it, not one snapshot of the store.**
  Each run is one read snapshot; across runs, a row is checked as it stood when its run reached it.
- **Q11: the window before siblings see a marker grows from at most 1 s** (the inline reading)
  **to many runs.** A sibling is held back by nothing until the marker exists, and the walk takes
  as many runs as the store needs. This is an accepted cost.

| # | Question | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|
| Q9 ⭐ decided | Should a sibling's commit between runs (`meta.seq` moving) restart the walk, as the epoch does? | **No, as built** (105): restarting on every commit would never end on a store a sibling is writing, and the logical walk reads each row as SQLite holds it now |
| Q10 ⭐ decided | Should a wipe or forget call be refused while a walk is owed? | **No, as built**: a wipe replaces the content, a damaged page it meets is a code like any other, and the epoch it moves restarts the walk on a store that is then nearly empty. Refusing would strand "forget this device" behind a check |
| Q11 ⭐ decided | One walk per app (built), or one shared position that any app's worker advances? | **Per app, as built**: no two processes write one file, and the fence is the app's own, like `COMMIT_FAILED`. The cost: two apps that both meet the damage each walk the store |
| Q12 ⭐ decided | What does the user see meanwhile? | **"Checking storage…"**, with no action offered: not "storage unavailable", and not the damaged-data export, which follows only a confirmed marker. Progress, if shown, is the unit and the run count (`progress()`), never a percentage, since the walk's length is not known before it ends. S0b-3 builds it |
| Q13 ⭐ decided | Does an app extension sharing its app's name share its walk file? | **Name the walk by the bundle (app and extension apart) at the binding**: today `appName` is whatever the host passes, and two processes of one name would write one file |

#### B.8.5 The user-visible state

While the walk is owed, this app's runtime is fenced `COMMIT_FAILED` (reads absent, writes throw),
and every rebuild's open answers `StoreBeingChecked`. The host (S0b-3) shows "Checking storage…" and
retries the open, which also schedules the walk again. Reaching the end clean lifts the fence: the
next open judges the store as any other. A confirmed walk makes the next open `Corrupt`, with
Control's export (§6). A walk that cannot advance (115), or that meets an entry it cannot order
(112), is shown as "Storage could not be checked", with the fence kept. It lifts at a new code, at a
sibling's wipe or replacement under it (119), or at the next launch. ⭐ *Since B.9 an index entry of
any class is stepped past (122), so only a walk that cannot advance is shown so; and a store of a
layout this build does not know ends the walk with no verdict (123), so what the user sees is the
open's own answer for it (the update surface for a newer layout).* The walk's length is about one run per 47,000 pages read
cold (Q0's figure), plus a run per small unit. Each run is admitted only with 4.22 s of protected
time at the placeholders. ⚠ Only a code from an access, the open or a job reaches the walk; a
checkpoint's code never does (113), so a live runtime whose checkpoint met a code serves on, and
nothing is shown.

### B.9 The hold watchdog, with the walk's three carry-overs (2026-10-16)

**What it is.** S0b-2's next item on the path to binding, bound nowhere: **the hold watchdog**
(§4.2.1, S8), which enforces `HOLD_MAX` on one transaction while protection is plentiful. Before it,
the chunk loops' stops and the budget were asked only between statements, so one statement that ran
long (a cold cache, a pathological plan) held the write lock as long as it ran. It lands with the
three items B.8's final re-review left on the confirmation walk, each required before the store is
bound: (112) a `type` that is not TEXT ended the walk for good; (121) an unreadable `meta.epoch` was
called damage on a layout this build may not know; a stalled walk was rescheduled by every open
every 5 s.

**Split off, and not built here:**

| Not built | Why not here | Where |
|---|---|---|
| The 30 s foreground checkpoint trigger | "while foregrounded" is the UIKit adapter's signal, which does not exist (B.5.3). A timer started by nothing tests nothing | S0b-2, with the adapter |
| The end-of-job checkpoint trigger | "before its token is released, when past `Wmax/4`" needs a job that writes. The worker's only job is the read-only walk (B.8); the `REPLACEMENT` run on the worker and the hosts' sync jobs are not built | ⭐ *built in B.11 (148), for the `REPLACEMENT` run* |
| The token-expiry interrupt on the watchdog's queue (§4.2.1: "the same serial timer queue that runs the token-expiry interrupt") | the queue exists (`ReplicaWatchdogQueue`); the expiry handler that would call it belongs with the entries wrapped and the adapter | ⭐ built in B.15 |
| A checkpoint's own deadline, `CKPT_MAX` (§4.2.1's watchdog table), on its copy and its rewind write | a different class with a different bound; its `RESTART` waiting is already sliced by `B_ckpt`, and the copy is interruptible per frame once something calls the interrupt | ⭐ *built in B.10* |
| The open's own write transaction and its read-only classification under the watchdog (§4.2.1's table: "classification retried (`StoreUnavailable`)") | the open's read/write half is a third transaction shape (`ReplicaOpener`), with its own failure verdicts; it is admitted with `HOLD_MAX` reserved (B.7) but not watched | ⭐ *built in B.10 (Q15)* |

#### B.9.1 What exists

| Piece | What it does | Where |
|---|---|---|
| The watchdog | `ReplicaHoldWatchdog`, one per registry (`ReplicaHandles.holdWatchdog`). `arm` at the write lock gives a `ReplicaHold` and puts `HOLD_MAX` on `ReplicaWatchdogQueue`, a serial queue of the process's own | `ReplicaHoldWatchdog.kt` |
| The hold | `enterStatement`/`exitStatement` bracket every statement: refused once the deadline has passed (by the timer, or by the clock if the timer is late); while bracketed, the deadline interrupts. `beforeCommit` refuses or disarms in one step under the hold's lock. `disarm` after a rollback. The 500 ms long-hold log at the disarm | same |
| The access | `SharedReplicaStore`: armed right after `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` returned, before the marker lookup and the `-wal` probe (as a chunk counts them). Every statement through `statement()`, and the epoch read, bracketed. A `SQLITE_INTERRUPT` the watchdog caused, or a refusal, is `HoldCeilingExceeded` with the handle fenced `COMMIT_FAILED` (rule (a)). The `COMMIT` refused or the watch disarmed before it is issued | `SharedReplicaStore.kt` |
| The job's chunk | `ReplicaReplacement`: armed with the chunk's own clock, at the same point. `Chunk.held` brackets every statement and the marker readings; `Chunk.beforeCommit` disarms. Either refusal or an interrupt is a `ChunkStop("HoldCeilingExceeded")`: rolled back, the run `Stopped`, the `REPLACEMENT` handle released, no runtime fenced | `ReplicaReplacement.kt` |
| `HoldCeilingExceeded` | now a `ReplicaAccessFailed(COMMIT_FAILED)`, with SQLite's `SQLITE_INTERRUPT` as its cause when it was an interrupt | `ReplicaVerdicts.kt` |
| The class-aware index keyset | positions carry `afterClass`; `indexSql(index, resumeIn)` resumes in any class; the position file is format 3 | `ReplicaConfirmationWalk.kt` |
| The rows' datatype checks | `ROWS` holds each row to `quick_check`'s two per-row checks of this table (`rowChecks`) | same |
| `NoVerdict` | a store of another layout ends the walk with nothing marked | same |
| The back-off | an open's reschedule of a stalled walk doubles per schedule up to `OPEN_RESCHEDULE_MAX_MS` | same |

#### B.9.2 Decisions made in implementation, for review

Numbered on from B.8.

122. ⚠⚠ **The index keyset is storage-class-aware, and the rows unit makes `quick_check`'s row
     checks** (carry-over (112)). Each fact below was read in the vendored `sqlite3.c` (3.53.4) and
     the ones marked *measured* were also run (system `sqlite3` 3.51.0, then the tests on the
     vendored build):
     - **Order.** The index orders NULL < INTEGER and REAL (by value, across both) < TEXT
       (BINARY) < BLOB (`sqlite3VdbeRecordCompare`, `sqlite3MemCompare`).
     - **What a TEXT-affinity column does to a bound value.** `type` has TEXT affinity and a bound
       parameter has none, so `sqlite3CompareAffinity` gives the comparison TEXT affinity, applied
       to the value. That leaves a TEXT or a BLOB as it is (`applyAffinity` converts numbers only),
       so **TEXT and BLOB resume exactly as before**: `type = ? AND rowid > ?`, then `type > ?`,
       bound with `bindTextBytes` or `bindBlob`. A BLOB sorts after every TEXT, so `type > ?` with
       a TEXT key reaches the BLOBs.
     - **Numbers cannot be bound that way.** The same affinity turns a bound 5 into '5'
       (*measured*: `type = 5` finds no INTEGER 5). They are compared through `+type`, which has no
       affinity (`sqlite3ExprAffinity` returns the `TK_UPLUS` node's own), so the comparison is
       numeric across INTEGER and REAL, as the index's is. ⚠ *Revised in the fix round (129):* one
       statement with no range, `+type > ?1 OR (+type = ?1 AND rowid > ?2)`.
     - **NULL cannot be found by `IS NULL`.** On a NOT NULL column `type IS NULL` is folded to
       false (`sqlite3ExprCanBeNull`), `+type IS NULL` included (*measured*: both find nothing). So
       the first round used `typeof(type) = 'null'` under `type < ''`. ⚠ *Replaced in the fix round
       (129):* the plain scan, with the NULLs already read stepped over in Kotlin.
     - **Why the rows unit changed too.** `quick_check` checks a **row's** datatypes ("Verify
       datatypes for all columns": (1) NOT NULL holds no NULL; (3) a TEXT column of a non-STRICT
       table holds no INTEGER or REAL), and it runs those for `quick_check` as for
       `integrity_check`. It checks no **index entry's** datatype. So a NULL or a number in a row
       is damage at `WHOLE` on a small store, and `ROWS` now says the same on a large one (it reads
       `typeof()` of each checked column); a BLOB in a row is no finding at either. An index entry
       of any class is no finding at either, and the walk steps past it. The verdict no longer
       depends on the store's size, which was the second fix round's reason to stop.
     - **What is gone:** `Read.Uncheckable` and the `Stalled` it gave; the doc comment that the
       keyset "cannot step past it soundly". **The cost:** an entry of the NULL or the numeric class
       re-reads the entries of its class before it on each run. Only damage writes either class
       (`UPSERT_SQL` binds `type` as text into a `TEXT NOT NULL` column), and a class too large for
       one run's worth stalls under (115) instead of spinning.
     - ~~What the tests pin rather than a guarantee: that `type < ''` returns the NULL entries.~~
       ⚠ *Gone with (129): no resume depends on the planner any more.*
123. ⚠⚠ **Only a store of this build's layout is judged by the walk** (carry-over (121)). The run
     reads `readMarker(...).layout` first; anything but `ReplicaSchema.LAYOUT` (newer, older, or
     none readable) ends the walk **with no verdict** (`ReplicaWalkOutcome.NoVerdict`): nothing
     marked, the position removed, the walk owes nothing, and this app's fence is lifted. The open
     then judges the store by its own rules, which refuse a layout they do not know and write
     nothing: a newer one is `SKEW` (the update surface), an older one `OlderLayout`, none readable
     its damage rule. This covers both cases the re-review named: the unreadable epoch (which (121)
     would have marked on a store this build cannot read), and a unit list that cannot even be
     prepared on another layout (`quick_check(<table>)`, the `ROWS` column list, `INDEXED BY`), which
     was `NotMade` at every run for good. **Terminal and not marking, stated and surfaced:** the
     worker hands `NoVerdict` to the host (`onOutcome`) and it is logged. Keeping the fence instead,
     as a `Stalled`, was not chosen: the user would see "could not be checked" where the store needs
     an update, and the open refuses the store anyway.
124. ⚠⚠ **The hold watchdog, as built.**
     - **One watch per transaction, armed at the write lock.** Its timer cannot be cancelled
       (`dispatch_after`), so a deadline that fires for a disarmed watch does nothing.
     - **An interrupt is only ever issued inside a bracket**, under the watch's lock, so it cannot
       land after the statement was marked ended. A stray flag would be harmless anyway: SQLite
       clears it at the next statement's start or prepare with none active (`sqlite3Step`,
       `sqlite3RunParser`), and the checkpoint that is the one call it does not clear for
       (§4.2.1) runs on a connection of its own.
     - ⚠ **An interrupt can be lost** for the same reason: one landing after the store bracketed a
       statement and before SQLite started it is cleared at the start. **So it is issued again**
       every `REINTERRUPT_MS` (50 ms, a placeholder) while the statement runs. Tested by firing the
       first one exactly there.
     - **The clock is checked as well as the timer** at every bracket and at `beforeCommit`: a late
       timer (a busy queue) never lets a statement or a `COMMIT` start past `HOLD_MAX`.
     - **`beforeCommit` refuses or disarms in one step** under the watch's lock, so the deadline can
       neither interrupt the `COMMIT` nor refuse it after it was issued. The `COMMIT`'s sync is R2.
     - **A chunk keeps its own clock check** (`Chunk.hold`, the tests' moved clock) beside the watch.
125. **A stalled walk's open-driven reschedule backs off** (the nit). The window is 5 s and, while
     stalled, doubles at each schedule an open dispatches, to `OPEN_RESCHEDULE_MAX_MS` (5 min, a
     placeholder); a new hand-off or a lifted stall resets it. A stalled run is cheap (the
     classification and the epoch), but it still costs a job token, a connection and that read, for
     as long as a host retries its open.
126. **(121) marks on one read-only snapshot** (the nit). The run's reading of `meta.epoch` is a
     single read transaction on a `CLASSIFY` connection, not two readings that agree. That is
     defensible because the run is itself the second reading of a code already met: (45)'s two
     readings are the access's code and this run.
127. ~~Two protection tests changed meaning, not assertions.~~ ⚠ *Superseded by (131):* the
     watchdog is off outside its own suite, and both tests are back to their original expectations.

**Fix round of the independent review (2026-10-16).**

128. ⚠⚠ **The watchdog never watches a ROLLBACK.** The access's error handling (`refuse`,
     `failed`, the confirmation) rolls back, and it ran inside the statement's bracket: the
     statement was still counted as running and the watch armed, so the 50 ms re-interrupt could
     land on the `ROLLBACK`. An interrupt can stop a `ROLLBACK` (the reviewer read it in
     `sqlite3.c`); the rollback then fails and the write lock stays held, in a nested access until
     the outer one ends. Now:
     - `statement()` and the epoch read mark the statement ended (and reset it) **before** any
       failure is handled;
     - `rollback()` disarms the watch **before** it issues `ROLLBACK`, and the corruption code's
       hand-off disarms before the confirmation closes the connection.

     Either alone closes the hole; both are kept, and each is pinned separately (M126, M127). The
     job's chunk was already right: `held` ends the statement before the transaction's handlers
     roll back. **Every SQLite call inside a watched transaction**, checked by grep: each is under
     `statement()` (the access) or `Chunk.held` / `Chunk.read` (the job, the marker readings and
     the schema validation included), except `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` (before the watch is armed),
     `COMMIT` (after it is disarmed, its sync is R2) and `ROLLBACK` (never watched, above).
129. ⚠⚠ **The NULL and the numeric resumes depend on no planner detail** (replacing part of (122)).
     The NULL resume `type < '' AND typeof(type) = 'null'` is semantically empty. It returned the
     NULLs only because SQLite skips NULLs at a range's start just for a nullable column
     (`bSeekPastNull`, `sqlite3.c` 165872 to 165875) and because the range's end term is consumed by
     the seek rather than evaluated again. A later SQLite changing either would have made the walk
     skip the rest of the NULLs and end `Clean`, on exactly the damage it exists for. **The same
     was true of the numeric resume's `type < ''` bound**, found while making this fix:
     evaluated as SQL, `OP_Lt` under TEXT affinity stringifies a stored number
     (`sqlite3VdbeMemStringify`), so `7 < ''` is false. Now:
     - **NULL** resumes on the plain index scan (`INDEXED BY objects_type ORDER BY type, rowid`,
       no `WHERE`), stepping over the entries up to `(NULL, afterKey)` in Kotlin and going straight
       on into the numbers, TEXT and BLOB;
     - **INTEGER and REAL** resume on one statement with no range,
       `+type > ?1 OR (+type = ?1 AND rowid > ?2)`, whose comparisons have no affinity and so are
       the index's own order (numbers by value, then every TEXT and BLOB, never a NULL);
     - **TEXT and BLOB** keep their seek. Read as SQL, `type > ?` with a TEXT key would also hold
       for a stored number whose text sorts after the key: a superset, never a subset. A planner
       that evaluated it as a filter could only make runs re-read entries (a stall), never skip
       one.

     ⚠ **The cost, named in the code:** `+type` is not sargable, and the NULL resume has no
     `WHERE`, so a run inside either class rescans the NULLs and the numbers before its key. A large
     NULL or numeric region (only damage writes one) can stall under (115); it cannot end `Clean`.
130. **A unit's start carries no class.** `walkUnits` and `bounded` moved to the next unit by
     clearing `afterKey` and `afterType` and kept `afterClass`. A position saved in the `SCHEMA`
     unit after the index therefore did not decode, and after a process death the walk started
     again from `WHOLE`. Both now go through `ReplicaWalkPosition.atUnitStart`, which clears all
     three.
131. **The watchdog is off in every iOS SQLite suite but its own.** `ReplicaProcess` holds the
     watchdog's timers and never fires them, and freezes its clock, so the ~300 other tests are no
     longer under a real-time 1 s ceiling on a host that has stalled for longer (B.8.6). Only
     `ReplicaHoldWatchdogTest` opts in, by firing the timers and moving the clock itself. The two
     protection tests of (127) are restored to their original expectations (the idle access
     commits), since they no longer need `HoldCeilingExceeded`. ⚠ A job chunk's own clock check
     (`Chunk.hold`, real time) predates this slice and stays as it was.

#### B.9.4 Tests and mutations

`ReplicaHoldWatchdogTest` (new, 8 tests since the fix round), every store made up, the watchdog's timer held by the test
and fired at the point each case is about:
- a statement running past `HOLD_MAX` is interrupted (a recursive count that only an interrupt
  stops; its own 5 s stop fails the test instead of hanging it), the access refused with SQLite's
  `SQLITE_INTERRUPT` as the cause, the handle fenced `COMMIT_FAILED`, everything rolled back;
- a block idle past it has its next statement refused before SQLite;
- and its `COMMIT` refused, never issued;
- the deadline firing as the `COMMIT` is issued neither interrupts nor refuses it, the watch is
  disarmed, and a stale deadline does nothing to a later transaction;
- an interrupt lost before the statement starts is issued again;
- a wipe chunk on a `REPLACEMENT` handle interrupted: rolled back whole, the run `Stopped`
  ("HoldCeilingExceeded"), its handle released, the live runtime not fenced; the deadline between
  two statements of the next chunk refuses the next one; the next run finishes the wipe;
- (fix round) the deadline firing as an interrupted read's `ROLLBACK` is issued finds the watch
  disarmed and no statement running, issues no interrupt, and the lock is free afterwards;
- (fix round) with the timer never firing, the clock alone refuses the next statement and the
  `COMMIT`.

In the fix round the walk tests also cover: a position at the start of the schema unit, reached
from inside an index key of every class, carries no class and round-trips; and the NULL and
numeric statements are plain covering scans that sort nothing.

`ReplicaConfirmationWalkTest` grows to 25 tests:
- the codec round-trips a key of every class and refuses one malformed for its class;
- the plan test covers every class's statements;
- the non-TEXT test is replaced by two: index entries of every class (NULL, INTEGER, REAL, TEXT,
  BLOB, the empty TEXT and BLOB among them) with every entry a run boundary, the union of keys
  reached equal to every entry and a run resumed inside every class; and a NULL, an INTEGER, a REAL
  in a row's `type` confirmed damage whether the store is read whole or ranged, a BLOB clean at both.
  The rows NULL and numbers are written through `writable_schema`, the declaration put back exactly;
- two layout tests: an unreadable epoch on a newer layout is `NoVerdict`, nothing marked; a newer
  layout whose index is gone ends the walk with no verdict, and the open answers `SKEW` with the
  file unchanged;
- the stall test checks the back-off (each gap double the last, to the cap) and its reset.

### B.10 The open under the watchdog, the walk judged by the open's rule, and `CKPT_MAX` (2026-10-16)

**What it is.** The maintainer's two decisions of 2026-10-16 in code, bound nowhere, with the two
items B.9's re-review left and one more S0b-2 item that needs neither the UIKit adapter nor S0b-3's
host:
- **Q15:** the open's read-only classification and its write transaction under the hold watchdog,
  as §4.2.1's table says. Either one past `HOLD_MAX` is a retryable `StoreUnavailable`, with nothing
  judged and nothing written.
- **Q16:** on this build's layout, the walk judges the store **by the open's own rule** before it
  reads a unit. A store missing a table or its index is damage there, as at the open, instead of
  `NotMade` at every run.
- **B.9's carry-overs:** a TEXT or BLOB resume under a plan that filters can no longer report an
  entry behind its start, and `isPast` is order-aware (B.9's claim that this would be "a stall" is
  corrected). One test now runs the production timer and clock to an interrupt, and the parked-access
  interplay two protection tests used to check is back as two opt-in tests.
- **Part C, a checkpoint's own deadline `CKPT_MAX`:** on its copy, its `RESTART` slices and its
  rewind write.

**Split off, and not built here** (B.9's list, less what this slice built):

| The token-expiry interrupt on the watchdog's queue | which statements an expiry stops depends on which entries the token covers, which is decided when the entries are wrapped (B.9's reason, unchanged). The queue and `CKPT_MAX`'s watch are ready for it | ⭐ built in B.15 (B.15.3 is which statements it stops) |
| The 30 s foreground checkpoint trigger | "while foregrounded" is the UIKit adapter's signal (B.5.3) | S0b-2, with the adapter |
| The end-of-job checkpoint trigger | still no job that writes on the worker: its one job is the read-only walk (B.8). The `REPLACEMENT` run needs S0b-3's host | ⭐ *built in B.11 (148): only the reopen after `Finished` needed the host* |
| `CKPT_MAX` as Control's wait after the marker before it copies a corrupt store (§6) | Control's snapshot has no phase (B.2) | with the snapshot |

| Piece | What it does | Where |

| The classification's watch | `readOnly(…, watched = true)`: armed once the read transaction has begun, the reading one bracket, disarmed before its `ROLLBACK`. A `HoldCeilingExceeded` there is the open's `StoreUnavailable` | `ReplicaCorruptionConfirm.kt`, `SharedReplicaStoreOpen.kt` |
| The open's write transaction's watch | armed right after `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` returned. Every statement bracketed, including the marker's re-read, the create, the validation and the two `meta` reads. Disarmed before each `ROLLBACK`, before a corruption code's hand-off closes the connection, and in the `finally` before the release. `beforeCommit` before the `COMMIT` | `SharedReplicaStoreOpen.kt` |
| `ReplicaHold.statement` | one bracket as an inline function: refused past the deadline, interrupted while it runs, the watchdog's `SQLITE_INTERRUPT` thrown as `HoldCeilingExceeded`, the statement marked ended before the failure reaches the caller | `ReplicaHoldWatchdog.kt` |

#### B.10.2 Decisions made in implementation, for review

Numbered on from B.9.

132. ⚠⚠ **The walk's verdict before the units is the open's, computed the same way** (Q16). In
     order:
     - ~~(123)'s gate first: a layout that is not this build's is `NoVerdict`.~~ ⚠ *Removed in the
       fix round (141): `classify` answers another layout itself.*
     - Then `classify(reading, build)`, the one function both halves of the open use:
       - `Skew` and `OlderLayout` are **no verdict**. The open refuses both with nothing judged
         damaged and nothing written, so `Skew` takes precedence over damage here as it does
         there (`classify`'s rule 1). This covers a newer build's store **on this very layout**
         (a service version above this build's), which (123)'s gate does not see. Validating it
         would mark a store the open would only answer with the update surface.
       - `Damaged` is damage, as the open's marker.
       - `Compatible`, `Behind` and `Updating` go on to `ReplicaSchema.validate`, whose finding is
         damage. These are exactly the verdicts after which the open validates: the write half for
         `Compatible`, the job's admission for the other two.
     - Then the epoch and the units, as before.

     **The build.** The walk needs one to judge versions, so the build that opened the store is
     carried into the walk through `ReplicaCorruptionConfirm` and `SharedReplicaStore`. A process
     runs one build, so the first caller's is kept. **The single snapshot** is defended as (126)
     is: the run is itself the second reading of a code already met. A store that the classification
     calls damaged (a negative `meta.seq`, say), which `quick_check` never reads, would otherwise end
     `Clean` and then be marked by the open; both now say damage. (121)'s epoch rule stays after
     this, and is now reached only for a `meta.epoch` that validation passed.
133. ⚠⚠ **No index position behind the start, by construction and by comparison** (B.9's first
     carry-over). Read as SQL, the TEXT resume's `type > ?` also holds for a stored number whose text
     sorts after the key. Under a plan that evaluated it as a filter, those numbers came back first.
     They are **behind** the start in the index's order, and a run bounded there saved a position
     behind it. `isPast` counted any change as progress, so the walk could go back and forth with no
     stall. It could never end `Clean` falsely: the extra entries are re-reads, never skips. B.9
     (129) called this "a stall", which was wrong. Now:
     - `walkIndex` steps over, in Kotlin, every entry at or before the resume point in the index's
       own order, whatever the statement returned. That subsumes the NULL skip of (129): inside the
       NULL class these are the NULLs already read.
     - `isPast` compares positions in that order. A position behind is never progress, even if a
       later change put one there.
     - The order (`ReplicaIndexKey`) is SQLite's (`sqlite3VdbeRecordCompare`, `sqlite3MemCompare`,
       `sqlite3IntFloatCompare`, 3.53.4): NULL; INTEGER and REAL by value, compared exactly (a 64-bit
       integer is never rounded to a double); TEXT by bytes then length; BLOB the same; then the
       rowid. The test checks it against SQLite's own `ORDER BY` over a column with no affinity.
134. **The classification's watch is one bracket around the whole reading.** The reading is SQLite
     calls only (`readMarker`), so an interrupt anywhere in it is sound. It is armed after `BEGIN`:
     a deferred `BEGIN` takes no read mark, and the first read does. It is disarmed in the `finally`
     before the `ROLLBACK` ((128)). A refusal or an interrupt is `StoreUnavailable`, caused by
     `HoldCeilingExceeded`, thrown before any verdict. It is never a corruption code, so neither of
     the two readings of `readAndJudge` writes a marker on it. "Retried" is the caller's retry, as
     for every `StoreUnavailable`: the open already holds its admission, and a retry inside it would
     double the hold. The other two users of `readOnly`, the walk and the corruption confirmation,
     are not watched (Q18).
135. ⚠⚠ **The open's write transaction under `HOLD_MAX`, as an access is, with one difference:
     there is no handle to fence.** The store is not handed out until the `COMMIT`, so rule (a) is:
     roll back, release the handle (the `finally` already does both), and throw a retryable
     `StoreUnavailable`. A fresh store interrupted mid-create is still empty, and the next open
     creates it.
     - **Every SQLite call in it, checked by grep:** every statement is bracketed; `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`
       comes before the watch is armed; `COMMIT` comes after `beforeCommit`; every `ROLLBACK`
       (the marker found, a sibling's change, and the release's) comes after a disarm.
       `requireStoreSettings` runs on the connection's open, before `BEGIN`, and is exempt like any
       open (§4.2.1).
     - **The create is one bracket** of a handful of statements. Fine: an interrupt anywhere in it
       rolls back the whole store-to-be.
     - **The marker's file work** (the lookup and the directory sync) is outside every bracket but
       counts against the hold, as an access's does. The next statement or the `COMMIT` is refused.
136. ⚠ **`CKPT_MAX` is a watch on the same watchdog, with its own bound.** ⚠ *Revised in the fix
     round (138): armed only in protected background time; in the foreground a copy runs to its end.*
     - It is armed once the checkpoint's own connection is open: an open's index rebuild is exempt
       (§4.2.1).
     - It brackets each `RESTART` slice, the rewind's `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` and its statement, and is
       disarmed before the rewind's refused `ROLLBACK` and as its `COMMIT` is issued.
     - On firing, the checkpoint is "skipped" (`NotReset`), which the design already calls safe:
       a retry re-copies nothing. It is never a corruption code, and it neither counts nor resets
       `checkpointCodesInARow`.
     - ⚠ **The stray flag of §4.2.1.** A `sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2` that is the connection's very
       next call returns `SQLITE_INTERRUPT` (results doc §11 (3)). Here it can only follow an
       interrupt this watch issued, and so a passed deadline, whose next bracket is refused anyway.
       The connection is closed at the end of the run either way.
     - **The value** is derived from two placeholders (`T` and `B_ckpt`), so it is a placeholder
       too (1,650 ms) until Q0 (i) and (p).
137. **The production timer is under test, and the parked access is back.**
     - One real-time test runs `ReplicaWatchdogQueue` (`dispatch_after`) and the monotonic clock,
       with `HOLD_MAX` = 200 ms and a statement held running. It asserts the interrupt came no
       sooner than `HOLD_MAX` and well inside 4 s, 20 times the bound, for a shared and heavily
       loaded host. ⚠ *Widened in the fix round (142): 30 s, the statement's own stop at 60 s.*
     - The two `ReplicaProtectionTest` expectations of B.9's first fix round return as two opt-in
       twins of the original tests. With the watchdog in real time, the access parked through an
       expiry-cut drain has its `COMMIT` refused before SQLite, and every other assertion of the
       drain is unchanged. The originals keep the watchdog off ((131)).

**Fix round of the independent review (2026-10-16).**

138. ⚠⚠ **`CKPT_MAX` bounds a checkpoint only in protected background time** (review #1, must
     be resolved before binding). In the vendored 3.53.4, `walCheckpoint`'s copy loop checks the
     interrupt at every frame and stores `nBackfill` only after the whole loop and its sync, so **an
     interrupted copy keeps none of its progress**. Bounded everywhere, a log at the ceiling whose
     cold copy takes longer than `CKPT_MAX` would be stopped at every attempt. That could come from
     a wrong `T`, a sibling's breach, or a log an older build left. Every write at the ceiling would
     then be `WalResetPending`, for good: the store could never be written again, where before a
     slow checkpoint was slow and then finished. Of the two remedies named:
     - **Chosen: no deadline in the foreground, `CKPT_MAX` in the background.** In the foreground,
       `remaining` is null (B.7) and nothing suspends the process mid-copy, so a copy that is making
       progress runs to its end: the case that wedges is the foreground's to finish. In protected
       background time the bound is what the admission was for. `RESTART` is admitted only with
       `remaining ≥ T + B_ckpt + S + 2·S_full + 2 s`, and `CKPT_MAX = 2·T + B_ckpt` stops a copy
       that has run twice its admitted `T`, inside the 2 s margin, before file locks can be held at
       suspension (`0xdead10cc`). ~~The state is read once, at the arm; a backgrounding mid-copy is
       covered by the backgrounding token, like any foreground work (§4.2.1).~~ ⚠ *Wrong, revised
       in (143): no quiesce can stop a running checkpoint and the token-expiry interrupt is not
       built, so the state is judged when the deadline passes.*
     - **Not chosen: bounding only `RESTART`'s waiting slices.** The waiting is already bounded by
       `B_ckpt` in 50 ms slices, and the copy is the one unbounded part. In the background it must
       stay bounded, so this remedy would have left the background case unprotected.
     - **Surfaced:** a background stop is counted (`ReplicaHandles.checkpointCeilingStopsInARow`,
       logged with the count, reset by a checkpoint that runs to its end), so a log this device
       cannot reset in the background is visible to the host.
139. ⚠⚠ **A REAL key compares as SQLite compares it** (review #2, a false `Clean`). Kotlin's
     `Double.compareTo` is a total order: −0.0 before 0.0, NaN last. `sqlite3MemCompare` calls −0.0
     and 0.0 equal, and the rowid decides. So `(−0.0, 7)` after `(0.0, 5)` read as "at or before"
     the resume point, and the skip of (133) stepped over it unread; `isPast` erred the same way. Now
     `<`, `>`, else equal. Measured in the test: SQLite keeps a bound −0.0's bits in a column with
     no affinity, and stores a bound NaN as NULL, so no NaN reaches the comparison.
140. ⚠ **The open's file work under the lock is exempt from `HOLD_MAX`, and refusals are counted**
     (review #3). §4.2.1's watchdog table already exempts "a marker or sentinel file" (no
     statement to interrupt; its syncs are R2), so B.10's counting the open's marker lookup and the
     create's directory `F_FULLFSYNC` against the hold contradicted the design. Now:
     - `ReplicaHold.exempt` brackets that file work. The clock check subtracts its time. A deadline
       that falls inside it waits for its end and is then armed again for what the hold had left;
       one that falls after it is pushed back by its time. A slow sync is no longer a refused open.
       It does lengthen the lock's hold by up to `S_full` (R2). The admission reserves `2 · S_full`
       for the marker's syncs, and the create's one directory sync fits within the 2 s margin.
     - ⚠ **What stays counted:** the statements, the validation among them. A cold open whose
       statements need more than 1 s is still refused, and to keep that from being a silent retry
       loop it is counted (`openHoldRefusalsInARow`, reset by a served open). From
       `OPEN_HOLD_REFUSALS_REPORTED` (3, a placeholder) in a row the log calls it out, as (115) does
       for a stalled walk.
     - An access's own marker lookup is unchanged: a `stat`, which syncs only on a marker found, and
       the access is then fenced anyway.
141. **The walk's layout gate is gone** (nit). It ran before `classify` and compared with
     `ReplicaSchema.LAYOUT`, so a store of ours with no readable `meta.layout` was `NoVerdict` in the
     walk and `Damaged` at the open: harmless, but against "never disagree". `classify` against the
     build answers every case: another layout is `Skew` or `OlderLayout` (no verdict), none readable
     is `Damaged`. ⚠ **A rule for whoever adds layout 2:** the layout change must land in one
     transaction with its DDL. An intermediate shape (new tables, old `meta.layout`, or the
     reverse) would fail validation on this layout's rules, and the walk and the open alike would
     mark it permanently.
142. **The real-time test's bound is 30 s** (nit), with the held statement's own stop at 60 s. The
     host has stalled for minutes; the test now asserts only that the production timer's interrupt
     arrives (no sooner than `HOLD_MAX`) before the statement would stop by itself.

**Second fix round, the re-review of `fa47629` (2026-10-16).**

143. ⚠⚠ **`CKPT_MAX` is judged when it passes, not when it is armed** (review #1, should-fix: it
     regressed against `aa14347` towards `0xdead10cc`). Decided at the arm, a checkpoint begun in the
     foreground stayed unwatched if the app was backgrounded mid-copy. A quiesce cannot interrupt a
     running `sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2`, and the token-expiry interrupt is not built, so the copy
     could hold its checkpoint and read locks into suspension. Now:
     - The watch is **always armed**, with `deferWhile = { gate.remainingMs() == null }`.
     - When the deadline passes in the foreground, it is deferred and asked again every
       `DEFERRED_RECHECK_MS` (100 ms, a placeholder): one timer tick per 100 ms of a long foreground
       copy, and at most that long past backgrounding before the interrupt.
     - The clock checks (the next slice, the rewind's statements, its `COMMIT`) defer the same way,
       so a foreground copy that ran past `CKPT_MAX` still writes its rewind.
     - `deferWhile` is the checkpoint's alone. Every write transaction arms with none, so `HOLD_MAX`
       still fires in the foreground as B.9 has it.
144. **An exempt window no longer pushes a deadline back twice** (review #2). When the timer fired
     inside a window, the re-arm used `limitMs − heldMs`, which already leaves out every window,
     but `extensionOwed` from an earlier window was kept and pushed the re-armed deadline back
     again. Example: windows 100–400 and 900–1200 at `HOLD_MAX` 1,000 gave 1,900 for 1,600. The
     re-arm now clears it.
145. **`beginExempt` asserts it does not nest** (nit): nothing nests a window, and a nested one would
     lose the outer one's start.

#### B.10.4 Tests and mutations

`ReplicaHoldWatchdogTest` grows to 14 tests (16 after the fix round). Every store is made up, and the timers are held by the
test unless it says otherwise:
- **Q15, the classification:** a classification read running past `HOLD_MAX` is interrupted; the
  open is a `StoreUnavailable` whose cause is `HoldCeilingExceeded` with SQLite's
  `SQLITE_INTERRUPT`, armed at `HOLD_MAX`, no handle left, nothing marked, the file byte-identical;
  and the next open is served.
- **Q15, the write transaction:** the open's write transaction interrupted mid-transaction leaves no
  store created and no handle, and the retry creates it.
- **Q15, a passed deadline:** past its deadline the next statement (the deadline passing at the
  marker lookup) and the `COMMIT` are each refused before SQLite, with no interrupt and nothing
  created.
- **The production timer and clock** interrupt a running statement no sooner than `HOLD_MAX`
  (200 ms) and well inside 4 s.
- **`CKPT_MAX`:** a checkpoint running when `CKPT_MAX` fires is interrupted and skipped. It is
  armed at `CKPT_MAX`, not `HOLD_MAX`, counts no corruption code, and its connection is released;
  the next checkpoint resets. A rewind write past the deadline is refused before SQLite and not
  committed, and the write lock is free.

`ReplicaConfirmationWalkTest` grows to 30 tests (32 after the fix round):
- **Q16, a missing index:** on this layout, a store missing its index is confirmed damage ("schema
  validation: missing schema object") whether it is read whole or ranged, and a twin store's open
  answers `Corrupt` with the same finding. Before this slice the first was `Clean` (`quick_check`
  does not see a missing index) and the second `NotMade` at every run.
- **Q16, the classification's damage:** a negative `meta.seq` (classification damage that
  `quick_check` never reads) is damage in the walk and at the twin's open alike.
- **Q16, `Skew` first:** on this layout, a store ahead of this build with an extra index is
  `NoVerdict`, nothing marked, and the open answers `Skew` with the file unchanged.
- **The filter plan:** a TEXT resume under a forced filter plan (`NOT INDEXED`) reports no number
  behind its start, and the position the bounded run saves is past the start. The premise is
  asserted first: under that plan `type > '1a'` returns the numbers.
- **The order:** index positions of every class, sorted by the walk's own order, come back in
  exactly SQLite's `ORDER BY` order. A position counts as past another exactly when it is later in
  that order, and a rows position by its rowid alone.

### B.11 The `REPLACEMENT` run on the worker (2026-10-17)

**What it is.** B.8's split-off `REPLACEMENT` run, bound nowhere, with the three items that waited
on it:
- **The run on the worker.** The job an open answered `Updating` with is handed to the worker. The
  worker runs it off the launch path, one run per dispatch, under one job token per run
  (`acquireForJob`).
- **`run` refusing a migration chunk outside the foreground** (B.2, B.3 (56)), asked by every chunk.
- **A run that counted** a migration failure (`MigrationRowFailed`): the worker holds that store's
  job until the next foreground.
- **The end-of-job checkpoint** (§4.2.1's third opportunistic trigger): before the job's token is
  released, when the `-wal` has passed `Wmax/4`.

**Why this slice, and why now.** The four candidates the brief named were checked against the doc:

| Candidate | Verdict |
|---|---|
| The entries wrapped, then the token-expiry interrupt | ⚠ **Blocked.** The entries are app code: the draft's §5.4 list, and Fit's recorder and Timeline's capture, which are still to be read. Each wraps its work in `withProtection` on a `ReplicaProtection` the app constructs, so they come with the binding and the UIKit adapter, and where the adapter lives was **Q4** (open when this slice was chosen; ⭐ decided 2026-10-17: `:tenshu-sdk-ios-core`). Which statements the general expiry interrupt stops depends on which entries a token covers, so it waits with them (B.9, B.10). ⭐ *What this slice does make well-defined is the interrupt for a **job's** own token: it covers its own run's connection. Split off below* |
| The end-of-job checkpoint trigger | It needed a job that writes. ⭐ **Built here**, on the `REPLACEMENT` run |
| The `REPLACEMENT` run on the worker without S0b-3's host | ⭐ **Built here.** B.8 split it off because "installing the runtime needs S0b-3's host". Only that last step does. The open's own contract (`ReplicaOpenResult.Updating`) already says that the host opens again once the job answers `Finished`, the way it does after the walk (B.8.5). So the run, its token and its outcome need no host; the reopen that installs the runtime is the host's |
| A migration chunk refused outside the foreground | ⭐ **Built here.** It belongs to the run above (B.8's split) |
| A wipe call holding one token for the whole call | **Not here.** `wipeAllObjects` is called by the forget and wipe callers, which only the binding slice changes. Its caller can be on the main thread, where a job's token is refused (86), so *where* the token is taken is part of that change (B.8's reason, unchanged) |
| Any other S0b-1 binding prerequisite that is pure code | **Larger, and none is a prerequisite of this one:** the row cache, `data_version` and catch-up (§2.6, §3); the schema-registry adapter to `ReplicaMigrationSteps`; the watermark with its Keychain items and the lost-commit check (§5.4); `schedule_lease` with `LeaseKeyTooLong`. See "what is left" below |

This was the smallest coherent PR that unblocks the most. One run on the worker carries three of
the items split off earlier, and none of it waits on a decision or on the phone.

**Split off, and not built here:**

| The token-expiry interrupt for a **job's** token: at expiry, interrupt the run's statement on the watchdog's queue (today the expiry only stops the run between chunks, and the 2 s drain covers a chunk of at most `chunkTimeStopMs` + `HOLD_MAX`) | now well-defined, but it needs the interrupt to reach the checkpointer's own watch as well as the chunk's. A small slice of its own | ⭐ built in B.15 (203) |
| The general token-expiry interrupt (for entry tokens) | which statements it stops depends on the entries wrapped (the adapter; ⭐ Q4 decided 2026-10-17) | ⭐ built in B.15 (200) |
| The 30 s foreground checkpoint trigger | "while foregrounded" is the adapter's signal | ⭐ built in B.12 |
| The worker's triggers (`kick()` at a foreground and a wake) and its serial queue | UIKit | ⭐ built in B.12 (the wake's own caller is PIO-7's) |
| A wipe call holding one token for the whole call | above | the binding slice |

Still bound nowhere until the binding |
